subtopic: ELLIOT LAKE
ELLIOT LAKE
speechtext: Is the government giving consideration to cooperating with a committee formed to investigate the economic status of Elliot Lake and. if so (a) what are the names of all officials and companies belonging to the committee (b) what sums of money will be made available for stockpiling uranium ore from Elliot Lake during the next four years?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ELLIOT LAKE
speechtext:
The government has been cooperating with a special committee formed to investigate the economic status of Elliot Lake. The names of the individuals who served on this committee are:
Hon. W. Benidickson, P.C., M.P.; Mr. Jack Davis, M.P.; Hon. R. W. Macaulay, M.L.A.; Hon. J. W. Spooner, M.L.A.; Dr. E. B. Gillanders, executive vice president, Rio Algom Mines Ltd.; Mr. W. P. Arnold, general manager, Rio Algom Mines Ltd.; Mr. John Kostuik, vice president and general manager, Denison Mines Limited; Mr. M. J. deBastiani, mine manager, Denison Mines Limited; Mr. John Metz, Stanrock Uranium Mines Ltd.; Mr. J. T. Gauthier; Mr. Jack Wellard; Mr. J. S. McLaren.
Following several meetings of this committee, and as a result of market investigations at home and abroad, the Prime Minister was able to announce on June 26, 1963 that:
The government, strictly as a short term measure, is prepared to buy, and to stockpile, the quantities of uranium that will enable certain mines to maintain present employment until July 1, 1964, at prices which will cover the operating costs of the mines to that date.
The companies concerned have been informed of this offer and the government believes that satisfactory arrangements can be negotiated with them. When this has been done, the proposal will be put before parliament for approval.
The three mines affected are Milliken and Denison mines at Elliot Lake and Faraday mine at Bancroft. These are the mines which could continue to operate economically but which, under present contracts, will close at dates between next month and the end of the winter.
The communities concerned will therefore be able to rely on the continuation of present employment until the end of the next school year.
This decision is an expression of the government's declared general policy for facilitating industrial adjustments.
The government is meantime vigorously exploring the opportunities for alternative employment that may be developed in these communities during the next twelve months. To attempt to bring this search to a satisfactory conclusion will be a priority activity for the department of industry, and its area development agency, whose establishment the government has proposed to parliament.

Further reference was made to the mine coverage and possible cost of this program by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in parliament on July 2, 1963. His remarks appear on pages 1729-1730 of Hansard for that date.
Please note the minister's statement to the effect that:
The government... is prepared to buy and stockpile . .. uranium ... until July 1, 1964, at prices that will cover the operating costs of the mines.
The outlay involved will "be of the order of $20 million".

PRESS RELEASES, RESTRICTIVE TRADE PRACTICES COMMISSION
speechtext: Since January 1, 1956, has there been any change in the style, content or amount of information contained in press releases from or about the restrictive trade practices commission relating to reports of that commission and, if so, what are the details about such changes, and the dates upon which each such change took effect, and the source of instruction, if any, to put the said changes into effect?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PRESS RELEASES, RESTRICTIVE TRADE PRACTICES COMMISSION
speechtext:
Yes. The form of press release issued when making public reports of the restrictive trade practices commission was changed at the time of the report concerning the manufacture, distribution and sale of metal culverts and related products which was made public on August 16, 1957. Press releases issued on and subsequent to that date, generally speaking, have set out the title of the report, how the inquiry was instituted, date of argument before the commission at which representations were made on behalf of the parties and the director, date of report and a statement concerning consideration of what further steps should be taken. Press releases prior to the above date, in addition to the foregoing material, generally speaking, included a summary of the report, the findings and recommendations of the commission and the names of the persons or companies found to have participated in activities which were the subject of the report. The press releases are releases of, and issued by, the Minister of Justice.
I should like to inform the house that having reviewed this matter it is my intention, in releasing future reports, to return to the more detailed form of press release used prior to August 1957.

"(a) The act should provide for a term of office for band councils of not more than three years with one third of the members elected each year.
(b)	All band members, who are otherwise qualified, should be allowed to vote at band elections and on any other matter affecting the band if present on the reserve when the election is held.

(f)	The act should provide for filling a vacancy in a band council as soon as possible after the vacancy occurs.

(h)	It should be the definite policy of government to move toward more self governing bands and to this end more bands should be given control of their revenue funds.

(f)	In accordance with the provisions of section 77(4) of the Indian Act, a special election may be held to fill a vacancy when such vacancy occurs in a band council more than three months before the date when another election would ordinarily be held. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of Public Works said last week that any statement concerning the world fair would be made to this house rather than to the press I wonder if, because of the week-end events, the minister might follow up the news published by the press with an announcement directed to the House of Commons?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. P. Deschateleis (Minister of Public Works):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO FINAL CHOICE OF SITE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, circumstances have not allowed us to postpone until today that announcement which was made inside the parliament buildings last Saturday, and which was broadcast on television and published in Canadian newspapers.
On the other hand, if the hon. member is not quite familiar with the situation, I shall be pleased to supply him with detailed information.
He remembers no doubt that we received only on Thursday and Friday, June 27 and 28, 1963, the reports from the engineers of the city of Montreal, as well as the official request from the Montreal authorities to proceed with the work. This means that we were able to study the voluminous reports within a week and to arrive at a decision, which was no easy task. That is why we had arranged to meet with the parties concerned in Montreal on Saturday, July 6.
Following the statement of the mayor of Montreal that, in his opinion, such a meeting would serve no useful purpose, we decided that this meeting was not only useful but also urgent, and I feel that the events justified our position in that respect.
Therefore, we invited the mayor of Montreal to come to Ottawa on Friday, July 5, with his engineers, and he complied with our request. The engineers discussed some of the difficulties among themselves and, at the end of those meetings, we found out that we could come to an understanding.
The hon. member gives me an opportunity at this stage to say that we succeeded on two very important points.
First, our engineers had opposed the construction of a breakwater as suggested by the authorities of the city of Montreal, because they thought that such works were not adequate to withstand the pressure exerted by the ice in the Laprairie basin. And since that


construction was necessary to prevent flooding in the Montreal harbour, the federal government judged proper to assume the responsibility of the construction of a breakwater of the type and nature suggested by our engineers.
The second important point we won and which was not mentioned in the city of Montreal engineers' report, is the fact that the engineers from four departments of the federal government, namely the public works department, the transport department, the St. Lawrence seaway authority, and the national harbours board, will assist the engineers of the city of Montreal and, if necessary, will revise their plans, exactly as was done with much success for the development of the St. Lawrence seaway.
I hope that my hon. friends of the official opposition will share our satisfaction to see that this world exhibition has now been launched and that it will be a great success, not only for the city of Montreal, but for the country as a whole because that venture is of interest to the whole country.
Mr. Speaker, before resuming my seat, let me tell my hon. friends that the events have shown that this meeting was not only useful but also urgent.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO FINAL CHOICE OF SITE

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO FINAL CHOICE OF SITE
speechtext:
I had invited the provincial secretary, Mr. Gerard Levesque, as well as Mr. Bienvenu and Mr. Carsley to the meeting which was to be held in Montreal on Saturday and was convened for the purpose of trying to assess the difficulties facing the two engineering groups. [Editor's note: text of the answer referred to is as follows:]
I would like at this time to make reference to the matter raised by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and recorded on pages 590-91 of Hansard for June 3, 1963, concerning the discharge of a young man from the R.C.A.F. on the grounds that he was a bad security risk.
2.	In view of the periodic reviews to which this matter has been subjected, I feel sure that this is the case to which he refers.
3.	On May 7, 1948, the R.C.M.P. were requested by the R.C.A.F. to conduct a security check on this young man, who was being considered for secret duties with the air force. Again, on December 6, 1949, they were requested to conduct an S.A. clearance on
Inquiries of the Ministry behalf of the N.R.C., with whom this young man had applied for a position, whilst still employed in the R.C.A.F.
4.	The type of security clearance required in the second case, called for a high level field investigation.
5.	Field investigation of this subject revealed that a communist organizational meeting had been held on his father's farm in 1937. Subsequently, however, after representation had been made on this young man's behalf, additional information came to light which corroborated the original findings in this case.
6.	In 1950, as a result of representations made on this man's behalf, the superior of the college from which the young man had been expelled informed the R.C.M.P. that in 1936 he had had occasion to recommend the young man for summer employment. This recommendation resulted in the superior being censored by a minister of the Saskatchewan government, who produced a newspaper clipping which reported that the young man had chaired a communist meeting in Regina the previous night. The young man, when summoned by the superior, to explain the report, admitted among other things that the report was true. Expulsion followed.
7.	In addition, the young man involved then corresponded through the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam with Hon. Stuart Gar-son. In his statement to the minister of justice the airman admitted "youthful indiscretions" at the age of 18 and approximately 20, and went so far as to identify three men who had visited his home as "farm union organizers". The men he identified were well known as prominent communists of that day, two of whom are currently active in the communist party of Canada. The first man was provincial secretary of the communist party in Saskatchewan, the second was also a member of the provincial committee of the communist party of Canada in Saskatchewan, whilst the third was a member of the Regina district committee of the communist party of Canada in Saskatchewan.
8.	The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, in correspondence with Hon. Brooke Claxton, minister of national defence in 1950, stated that the young man had been duped into attending a three day conference in Regina, Saskatchewan, in 1937 of a communist front organization known as the league for Spanish democracy and that his name had subsequently got on the mailing list of this organization, causing him to receive literature and further invitations. This information was unknown to the R.C.M.P. at the time and was volunteered by Mr. Douglas.
9.	Again in 1950, in correspondence with Hon. Stuart Garson, the hon. member for

Inquiries of the Ministry Burnaby-Coquitlam stated that the young man had been duped into attending some communist meetings in 1937 and 1938, under the pretence they were going to help the loyalist government in Spain.
10.	With the investigation continuing, the superior of the young man's ex college was again interviewed and he reported that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam had informed him that he had personally interviewed the young man and had demanded of him why he had not mentioned his association with a particular man and the recruiting of persons for the Spanish civil war.
11.	The man referred to was a well known self admitted communist, and head of the communist "Friends of MacKenzie-Papineau Battalion" and section organizer of the communist party of Canada, Shaunavon district.
12.	The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has also made reference in the house to a photostatic copy of a letter which he possesses dispatched to the then minister of justice by the reverend father in charge of the school. I too am in possession of such a copy, and if my hon. friend will refer back to the letter he will discover that while pleading for the government to reinstate this man in the R.C.A.F., the reverend father includes the sentence "not in his old post of course".
13.	My hon. friend has alleged that the R.C.M.P. in this instance have confused communist activities with legitimate C.C.F. activities, and that as a result of their having misconstrued this information the young man has lost employment three times, his employer being informed inside of a month that this man is a bad security risk, and has been reduced to selling door to door in order to earn a living, meanwhile nursing an ulcer from worry and tension.
14.	However, according to our information the young man was not expelled from his college for C.C.F. activities, although two other students were expelled for this reason a year earlier, and the cases may have become confused. Again, the young man far from being hounded from job to job and being forced to sell from door to door has been apparently happily employed for the past 11 years with a provincial government. Finally, the principal of the college has not, as alleged by my hon. friend, cleared this man completely, but maintains his original stand.
15.	In summarizing governmental action in this matter, I must stress that the representations made on this young man's behalf have previously been considered by Hon. Brooke Claxton and by the Hon. Stuart Garson, while Mr. M. J. Coldwell acting on behalf
[Mr. Chevrier.l
of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has seen a summary of the information on file. In addition, the hon. gentleman who has raised this matter will recall, I'm sure, participating in a conference with ex-commissioner S. T. Wood and justice minister Gar-son on this subject.
16.	It will be seen therefore that this matter has received a great deal of attention over the years, based upon the representation of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam.
17.	This is a case where information as known to the R.C.M.P. was passed to the R.C.A.F. and N.R.C. who decided to take certain action. In the periodic reviews, additional information has been gathered to support that originally supplied. The information indicates that this is not a case of mixing up communist activities with legitimate C.C.F. activities, as alleged by the hon. member.
18.	Under all these circumstances I do not feel that the question of security risk in this case could have been resolved in any other way except in favour of the government.
19.	I hope that once and for all we can close this case and accept the word of the young man himself, who it is alleged does not want to become a "cause" and who wishes to remain happily in the job where he has been employed for 11 years. Any more publicity in this matter, instead of assisting the young man to settle down, could possibly disrupt the career which he has made for himself, since being discharged from the R.C.A.F. some 13 years ago,
20.	Finally I should like to say that this case has been exhaustively reviewed on a number of occasions by at least two former ministers of justice. We all share the objection of the hon. member to the thought of injustice in any such case and are seeking all possible ways to avoid it, but I am satisfied there was no injustice in this case, having regard to the legitimate interests of security. Under these circumstances I feel the matter should now be considered closed.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COUNCIL MEMBERSHIP, NAMES OF TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in rising to introduce this resolution on the amendments to the Northwest Territories Act I hope you will not find me out of order if I also refer in passing to the resolution respecting the establishment of Nunassiaq territory, which stands
28902-5-123
Northwest Territories Act as No. 7 on the order paper. As hon. members will understand, the two measures are very closely interrelated and they contemplate the division of the present Northwest Territories to make two new territories, the one on the west to be called Mackenzie, and the one on the east and far north to be called Nunassiaq.
At this point I would like to warn those who from time to time have indicated that they would prefer another name, that the name Nunassiaq was selected by the residents of that area, and it is the Eskimo name for "Beautiful Land."
On the mainland the dividing line between the territories will be the 105th meridian, which is roughly two thirds of the way from the Yukon boundary to Hudson bay. Mackenzie territory will also include Banks and Victoria islands, which are closely associated with the western mainland. The other islands of the Canadian Arctic will form part of Nunassiaq.
The legislation also provides for an elected majority on the council of Mackenzie territory, and for other changes which will have the effect of increasing the control exercised by the people of the present Mackenzie district over their own affairs.
We will later be considering the Nunassiaq resolution and bill, and at this stage I would only say that the legislation for Nunassiaq also contemplates increased local participation in government in accordance with the circumstances of that area.
In order to put this legislation in perspective I think it would be useful for me to review very briefly the history of territorial government in Canada. Almost since confederation the federal government has had to provide for the administration of very large areas on our frontiers. Although perhaps it is not generally recognized, we in Canada have a good deal of experience and have established our own practice in dealing with these questions. Various experiments have been tried over the years since 1869; some have been more successful than others. From the beginning, however, three fields consistently reappear.
The first thing is the recognition of a federal responsibility for these areas of great expanse and small population. The federal government has always accepted the role of a trustee, both for the people of all Canada who own the land and resources, and for the future residents of these areas, who will take over responsibility for them when the population has grown to the point where even provincial status can be contemplated.
The second thing has been a steady devolution of authority to local or territorial agencies as the population grows and substantial, settled communities develop. This

Northwest Territories Act pattern can be seen in the old North-West Territories after 1875, in the Yukon Territory early in this century, and in the present Northwest Territories over the past 15 years.
Finally it has been accepted that the forms of government should, as far as possible, accord with that British constitutional practice which is represented in our own parliament and government. In the present Northwest Territories, as in the old North-West Territories, there has been an attempt to recognize interdependence of the executive and the legislature. The amendments to the Yukon Act, which were passed in this house just three years ago, also reflect this accepted tradition.
The present Northwest Territories are what was left over from the old North-West Territories when the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan were established in 1905 and the provinces of Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec were enlarged to their present size in 1912.
The first large influx of population into the territories did not occur until gold was discovered at Yellowknife in the 1930's. In Yellowknife there was apparently some considerable and understandable dissatisfaction with the Ottawa council, but the war intervened and no changes were made at that time.
Developments after the war were reflected by substantial changes in the membership of the Northwest Territories council and in its activities. The first resident of the Northwest Territories was appointed to the council in 1946, and in 1951 the interests of people living in the territories were recognized when federal legislation provided for the election of three representatives from constituencies in the Mackenzie district. In 1954 the number of elected members was raised to four, continuing to provide representation for all the district of Mackenzie, but not for Keewatin or Franklin.
Many hon. members will be aware of the increasing activity of the Northwest Territories council since that time. The legislative fabric of the territories has been largely overhauled. Revised ordinances of the territories were published in 1956 to bring up to date the old body of laws which had been inherited from the North-West Territories of 1905. A conscious effort has been made, and today is substantially complete, to put the legislative, financial and administrative arrangements for government of the territories on a basis that would lend itself over the years to a smooth evolution toward provincial status. The present bill is a further step in that evolution.
The present legislation reflects a formal resolution of the Northwest Territories council which carries the support both of elected and

appointed members. The resolution was forwarded to the federal government following the council session in January 1962, and was accepted in principle by the government of that time.
With the consent of the committee, Mr. Chairman, I would like to table the resolution, since the legislation before us is designed to reflect the recommendations contained in it. I suggest that this resolution is so important to the matter we are discussing that I would like to have the consent of the house to have it printed in Hansard.

maintopic: RESOLUTION CONCERNING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW TERRITORIES IN THE NORTH

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: RESOLUTION CONCERNING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW TERRITORIES IN THE NORTH
speechtext:
As far as Mackenzie territory is concerned, the council recommended the boundaries which I mentioned earlier, and suggested a form of government similar in most respects to the present government of the Northwest Territories. For this new territory they suggested that the council should consist of nine members, of whom initially five should be residents of the territory, elected by the residents of the territory, and four should be non-residents appointed by his excellency the governor general in council. They further asked that the seat of government should be within the territory, and that the commissioner should be resident there.
It seems unnecessary for me at this resolution stage to enlarge at length on the council's statement. The plain fact is that the present Northwest Territories are so large and so diverse that it is exceedingly difficult for one government adequately to look after the needs of all the people. Frobisher Bay on Baffin island is as close to the United Kingdom as it is to the Yukon-Northwest Territories boundary. It is as far from the 60th parallel to the northernmost part of the territories as it is from here to New Orleans.
Beyond this, the people of the Mackenzie district have for many years been dissatisfied with the fact that the seat of government of the territories is in Ottawa. This resentment reflects not only a commendable measure of local assurance but also the difficulty which they have experienced in doing business with a government so far away. They feel, and I am sure every hon. member would agree, that they would be better served by a government which had its headquarters in the territories where it could remain in closer touch with local conditions and local needs.
At this stage, Mr. Chairman, I would like to point out that in the populated Mackenzie district we have found over half the population is living in the five settlements of Fort Simpson, Fort Smith, Hay River, Inu-vik and Yellowknife. A total of 8,000 of the population of 16,000 live in these five communities, which indicates that in the vast expanses of the north country there is seemingly a move toward urbanization, as there is in the rest of Canada. This indicates the necessity of having government in the area because, in the type of services required in

Northwest Territories Act these communities and the amenities attendant thereto, the people feel it is important they have authorities living there who can make decisions instead of authorities who come from Ottawa to make decisions.
The division of the territories is a prerequisite to the establishment of a resident commissioner and seat of government in the Mackenzie district. The seat of government is now in Ottawa simply because it is easier to reach any part of the territories from there than it is from any centre within the territories. Unless the territories are divided, the costs of operating a resident government would be exceedingly high, and it would be very difficult indeed for such a government adequately to reflect the needs and wishes of all the people throughout this vast area.
On second reading of the bill there will, of course, be an opportunity to discuss in more detail the considerations which led the council to frame their recommendation and which led both the present federal government and its predecessor to accept it. Hon. members will be better able to discuss these questions when they have the text of the bill before them. Accordingly I do not propose to deal with them in greater detail at the present time.
Mr. Chairman, I want to make some personal observations because it was my good fortune, in spite of the circumstances under which I went there, to visit Hay River and Fort Simpson at the time of the devastating flood. I am going to say that I found among the people there a mixture of very great responsibility and indomitable courage. I am quite certain those people possess these qualities because they are living there, and I think if they did not possess these qualities they would not be living there. I think the point has now been reached when we can say, though we keep the reservation always that the national government of Canada will have to assist those territories in the future as they have in the past, that the time has arrived to give them the maximum possible amount of self-government. The legislation which we propose as a result of this resolution will be a move in that direction.
We are discussing today, Mr. Chairman, not the bill itself but the resolution, which provides "That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Northwest Territories Act". I suggest to you, sir, that it is reasonable and proper for this house to give full and sympathetic consideration to the considered recommendations of the Northwest Territories council, which represents in its membership the people who will be most immediately affected by this measure and to which parliament has delegated much of our
[Mr. Laing.l
responsibility to make laws for the government of the northern reaches of Canada.

maintopic: RESOLUTION CONCERNING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW TERRITORIES IN THE NORTH
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am pleased that the resolution which has been brought before the house provides an opportunity for the discussion of northern affairs. It is some time since the house or a committee of the house had an opportunity to examine in some detail the developments that have taken place in the north, the area north of the 60th parallel. I think this occasion provides the ideal opportunity for such a widespread discussion, inasmuch as it is a proposal which contemplates legislation that is forthcoming largely because of the changes that have taken place in the north during recent years. There has been a tremendous upsurge of development. In other words, it is possible to say that at long last the north has come into its own and is now recognized as an integral part of Canada.
A northern development policy was deliberately embarked upon by the former administration. One of the first proposals which gave rise to the resolution which we have before the committee came from the former prime minister, now the Leader of the Opposition, who right from the outset of his administration indicated that he was fully aware of the necessity of Canada occupying this vast territory in her frontier. The Leader of the Opposition, when he was prime minister visiting the Northwest Territories back in July of 1961, appeared before the Northwest Territories council which at that time was in session. In his remarks to the council he included the following words:
I was particularly interested in one view that you expressed:

That was referring to a view that had been expressed by the council:
More and more the council believes that to a greater extent than ever before, self-government should be made available to the people in the north, and I'll join with you in that. Already the field has greatly widened the responsibilities of the council, and I can assure you of this fact: that having seen at first hand something of the achievements of the past, something of the things that have already been done, anything that you may suggest-and the members of the council-to increasing the field of your responsibility, and also providing, to a measure not before known, of selfgovernment, will receive my warmest approval and support.
Mr. Chairman, that was one of the early formal statements made on the matter. As I look back in the records I find that as early as April 1958, under the then minister of northern affairs and national resources, the present hon. member for Qu'Appelle, and the then prime minister, the main thesis deriving from the program of northern development that had been already launched at that early period in the new administration's activities was the necessity of granting greater local government and autonomy to the areas north of the 60th parallel.
I pay this tribute to the Leader of the Opposition because not everyone agreed with him that the time had come and was ripe for accepting Canada's heritage in every respect in these million and a half square miles which we now know constitute a part of Canada's rich heritage. He was the first prime minister to travel extensively north of the 60th parallel. That was necessitated because of the many official openings that took place in the north, the completion of the microwave network system of communications, the opening of roads to resources, the opening of the new townsite of Inuvik and the other activities that have been going on during recent years.
But as I say, this has not always been the viewpoint of many in this House of Commons or many across the country; there was considerable resistance when it was first put forward. It is obvious today in this house, on the part of the new government and all hon. members of the house, that there is common agreement that the time has come for a major forward step in recognizing the role played by the Northwest Territories in our system of confederation. This is a far cry from the days when the policy of the former administration was criticized in a rather flippant way as being a policy of building roads from igloo to igloo, and other observations to the effect that it was the result of a distorted or blurred vision. That vision has more than justified itself, and it bears out the truth of the scriptural injunction that where there is no vision the people perish.

Northwest Territories Act building roads from igloo to igloo. That is a matter of record, and it parallels in history the comment which was made when the government of Sir John A. Macdonald first sought to penetrate the Northwest Territories by building the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Liberal party of that day referred to the construction of the C.P.R. as building a railroad which would go from wigwam to wigwam.
This suggests that political parties do not change their fundamental orientation in their approach to national development. I remember another statement-and I am sure the hon. member for the Yukon will bear me out in this-that we were spending money in the north like drunken sailors.

maintopic: RESOLUTION CONCERNING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW TERRITORIES IN THE NORTH
speechtext: That was the present Prime Minister.

maintopic: RESOLUTION CONCERNING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW TERRITORIES IN THE NORTH
speechtext:
I think the hon. member for the Yukon will be taking part in this discussion later, so I will leave this aspect for him to deal with. To return to the circumstances which have made possible this very happy occasion in the House of Commons, let me say that one of the reasons the north was neglected for so many long years was our failure to appreciate that Canada, geographically and politically, is an indivisible entity. Professor Morton of the University of Manitoba in a recent paper put his finger on the point precisely when, in summing up an article on the prospects of northern development, he came to the conclusion that Canada is a northern nation with a northern heritage and a northern destiny.
This has always been true; it is not a recent discovery. There have been those right back to the days of Voltaire who have referred to eastern Canada, the part of Canada which was then known, as the land which God must have given to Cain, because it was so forbidding, so formidable in terms of its geography. We must recall that 75 per cent of Canada, in fact the heartland of Canada, is made up of the pre-Cambrian shield and this is rugged, rocky terrain which requires the best kind of pioneering citizens for its development; and we have had them in all generations since Canada was first occupied. Canada has been fortunate in its pioneering spirits. The outward expansion of our country has always been oriented into the northwest.
I was intrigued when I went to Halifax to discover-and the hon. member for Halifax, who is still the mayor of that city will bear me out on this point, I am sure-that Halifax still bears with pride a name by which it has long been designated, "guardian of the north". There is real recognition that the orientation of Canadian development was ever onward into the northwest. I was at

the Keefer terminal opening at the head of the lakes a year ago and I was most interested to find that the good citizens of Fort William and Port Arthur refer to their towns as "the gateway to the northwest". And they are very close to the Canadian-United States border.
This trend to the north is a fact evident from our history, but very often down through the years we have acted as though it had no basis in actuality. Thus when Saskatchewan and Alberta were carved out of the territories in 1905 many voices of doubt were raised. We remember it was just a decade or so before 1905 that criticism was raised of the national policy of building communication into the Northwest Territories at all. It was said that this region would only be good for buffalo and Indians and that we would be building a railroad which would not even pay for its axle grease. These are matters which are reported in Canadian history.
Now compare Canada's geographical position with that of the United States. The heartland of the United States is the Mississippi valley, and in geographical terms the differences between the patterns of development in Canada and in the United States can be partly explained by the topography and geography which we inherited.
I think this occasion also provides a wonderful opportunity to pay tribute to one of the first Canadians who recognized the potential of the Canadian north. I refer to the late Vilhjalmur Stefansson, who was bom in that part of Manitoba from where the Secretary of State comes.

maintopic: RESOLUTION CONCERNING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW TERRITORIES IN THE NORTH
speechtext:
No, he was bom at Ames, Manitoba, in an Icelandic community which was then part of the northwest territories. If I recall my history correctly-I am aware that the Secretary of State is a former professor of history from Manitoba, so I would not want to debate with him on this particular point-I recall that Arnes, Manitoba, was the birthplace of Mr. Stefansson, and, as I say, at that time it was part of the Northwest Territories. He was a member of a pioneering Icelandic family and he died last August full of honours for his outstanding work connected with the north. The exploration in which he was concerned took place in the early part of the century. He later became a lecturer and a savant at Dartmouth University in New Hampshire.
Stefansson was one of the first to appreciate the potential of the area with which this resolution deals. He received support for his exploration of 1912-18, from the government of Sir Robert Borden, which advanced

him up to $300,000, a substantial sum of money. The appeal for government support was first turned down, and it was only after the personal intervention of Sir Robert Borden, who in the tradition of Conservative prime ministers had enough wisdom to believe that the vision of Stefansson had some tangible significance, that the government of that day contributed that comparatively large sum of money. It was that expedition that produced one of the great works of Stefansson, the book entitled "The Friendly North". It is interesting that the name of the proposed new territory, Nunassiaq, literally translated means "the beautiful land". Following Stefans-son's expedition of 1912-18, he wrote of his experiences in "The Friendly North", a book which I have no doubt is well known to hon. members interested in northern matters. It was this new interpretation of the north which changed the whole outlook on the forbidding, formidable, unfriendly and cruel north. Unfortunately, the Canadian government did not continue to support Stefansson as had the Borden administration, and a good many of his contributions were directly lost to Canada. He moved across the border and established his northern institute at Dartmouth University.
Let me mention one or two of the ideas put forward by Stefansson over 40 years ago, just to show how visionary they were. He pioneered the idea of working from floating ice floes. Indeed, this is how he carried out a good part of his expedition. This idea was later taken over by the Soviets, and they have been using it with increasing enthusiasm during the past decade or so. During that time Canadian research in the north dropped to a very low ebb and is only now stepping up in tempo once again. He suggested the trans-polar route for aviation, which has become a reality in our time, and the feasibility of using submarines under the ice to tackle the transportation problem of the Canadian Arctic. This, as we know, became a fait accompli a year or so ago when a nuclear submarine of the United States navy was able to travel under ice all the way to the north pole.
But, Mr. Chairman, more important, it was the explorations of Stefansson which established beyond all shadow of a doubt the sovereignty of Canada over the Canadian archipelago. We owe a great debt to this Canadian who originally came from Manitoba. I speak as a Manitoban with some sense of pride in this regard. It is in the tradition of Canada, Mr. Chairman, that a good many of the pioneering developments in the north of Canada have originated from this province. It is still the only province with a railway on its arctic coast, and it will be for a long
Northwest Territories Act time to come. The development of northern Manitoba has always been of the pioneering kind.
To conclude this tribute to Mr. Stefansson, I might say he anticipated the mineral discoveries and the oil explorations and discoveries now being made. He talked about roads to resources and railroads to resources. He talked about modern communications, as I have already indicated. He even considered the possibility of tourism in the Canadian Arctic and sub-Arctic. Hence the title of his book "The Friendly North". All these things have now been realized.
I am not going into a long recital of what has been accomplished in the past few years, but in the area of oil exploration 123 million acres of the Canadian Arctic and subArctic are now under permit. This is more than any other province in Canada. It is hoped that there will be four more wells drilled in the Canadian archipelago during the present year. There have been discoveries of rich iron ore deposits inside the arctic circle which are so promising that California Standard, which made the discoveries, have formed a subsidiary company, Crest Exploration, with a view to exploiting and developing these resources. I do not want to be too visionary but it is not beyond the realm of possibility, with iron-ore deposits and oil and gas nearby that we might have in the not too distant future a Pittsburgh of the north based on a smelting operation there. Even on Baffin island a rich iron ore deposit was discovered last August, rich both quantitatively and qualitatively. The roads to resources and the microwave link-up now extending from the arctic coast to the Mackenzie delta, the northern research co-ordination centre now under construction at the Mackenzie delta, and the Pine Point railway which will cross north of latitude 60 next year, if it is up to construction schedule, are just a few of the developments which have given rise to the proposal we now have before us. Perhaps most of the developments mentioned are in the western Arctic, but the same pattern is unfolding in the eastern Arctic.
I should say a word about tourism in the north, because there has been some misunderstanding on this point and criticism still continues. It can be said, I think, that already tourism is the second most important economic aspect north of the 60th parallel. Why? Because the great desire of the tourist is to get away from the booming, buzzing confusion of the big cities and out into the wilderness and wide open spaces. North of the 60th parallel there is space in abundance and breathtaking beauty. In fact, everyone to whom I have spoken who has travelled

It is estimated that last summer 18,000 people visited Dawson City almost as many as crossed the trail of '98 during the great gold rush. At least $2 million in revenue was derived from the tourist industry in that important part of the northern area of Canada. Camp sites and picnic grounds as well as commercial motels are now springing up along the entire length of the Mackenzie highway. In the area of resource development this is a tremendous economic asset and it applies with equal significance to all parts of the north.
Let me move now to the most important area, human resource development, which is the subject of the current debate. There has been equal progress in the area of human affairs as well. For example, there is the spurt in education. The vote was given to the residents of the eastern Arctic for the first time in 1962. The hon. member for the Yukon was instrumental in promoting this development. It was received with a certain amount of misgiving because it was said that these people were not ready for the federal vote. However, they exercised their federal franchise with enthusiasm and wisdom during the past two elections. The anomaly in this respect is that they do not yet have the territorial vote.
As the minister indicated, the governmental situation in the Northwest Territories has long been somewhat of an anomaly because the people living in that part of Canada have never had the full benefits of the British traditions upon which our governmental system in Canada is founded. This resolution preceding the intended legislation provides a golden opportunity to bring Canada up to date in this regard. I am not going into the record, though perhaps the hon. member for Yukon will; but arrangements that were regarded as temporary have tended to become permanent; and now as we move this long step forward-

maintopic: RESOLUTION CONCERNING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW TERRITORIES IN THE NORTH
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall be very brief, and I appreciate the words of the leader of the house. Usually we are still on questions at this time of the day, so I shall be as brief as possible under the circumstances. There are just one or two observations I wish to make concerning the resolution which, as the minister has indicated, is based on the recommendation of the Northwest Territories council made in January, 1962. I think it provides us with an opportunity to overcome some of the anomalies that have prevailed in the government of the north for far too long. The only suggestion I should like to make as we consider the resolution is that we make certain that we are moving to do what everyone wants to have done in this legislation. There have been some misgivings on this score.
The former prime minister, now Leader of the Opposition, visualized this as a step forward in local and self-government for the territories. Following the recommendation from the Northwest Territories council certain representations were made. The mayor of Yellowknife, for example, wanted to be heard on this important matter. When I was the responsible minister I carried on quite a lengthy correspondence with him and suggested that he take the matter up with the Northwest Territories council. He then approached the former prime minister and received a commitment from him that when this legislation came before the house he would have a chance to be heard before a parliamentary committee. I should like to refer to an editorial dated July 1961 in the News of the North which, incidentally, the mayor of Yellowknife edits. In it he said:
So we're going to have a new territory. But let's have it governed so that it will represent the people of the north more adequately, so that it will not he dominated by the voice of the department of northern affairs.
It is interesting that this harks back to the same theme that was voiced in the 1930's when people like Jock McMeekin, the editor of the Yellowknife Blade, were talking about the bureaucratic clique that was supposed to handle the administration of the north. In 1961 Mayor Horton of Yellowknife put forward almost the same thesis. I think it should also be noted that since the recommendation

came forward from the territories council an important political change has taken place. As I have already indicated, the people of the eastern Arctic have the federal vote and in my opinion they have exercised their franchise with keen understanding. Yet they are faced with the anomaly of not having the territorial vote and they were not consulted and given the opportunity to be heard through the territorial council with regard to the proposals now being placed before the house.
As we move forward with this step that is so important to the north, I should like to suggest that the opportunity be given to the mayor and council of Yellowknife to be heard, as was promised, and for representatives from the eastern Arctic to be heard if they so desire. If they have the franchise so far as federal government matters are concerned, certainly they should also have it with respect to territorial matters. I hope that the legislation will take this fact into consideration. The hon. member for the Northwest Territories has already made this proposal in the form of a question in the house. Unfortunately he is absent today attending the meetings of the Northwest Territories council in Inuvik, but I am sure that if he were here he would renew his request.
Let me conclude by saying that the fundamental purpose of this resolution as I understand it is to provide for local control and local responsibility. This was one of the recommendations of the Glassco report. During recent years we have tried, within the framework of the existing legislation, to give the Northwest Territories more and more local responsibility and control. We certainly must be sure that this is the intent and purport of the legislation that will be brought in when the resolution has been given approval by this committee.
The central government of Canada has played an increasingly dominant role in directing the growth of the Canadian economy. This has been especially true of the frontier, by the very nature of the circumstances. The former government, in many ways that I have not time to go into now, tried to redress this imbalance in the west, in the maritimes as well as in the north. It is also a truism that in a free, democratic, pluralistic society, organized groups are always active and vocal. They must be given an opportunity to be heard. I trust that as we move forward with these measures, they will be shaped to assure that everything done is in the best interests of all the people in the north. The best way to do this is to provide them with an opportunity to be heard on these important matters.

maintopic: RESOLUTION CONCERNING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW TERRITORIES IN THE NORTH
speechtext:
My remarks will be brief, Mr. Chairman, because I should like to co-operate with the wish of the house leader to get this resolution through so that the bill may be passed to enable the Northwest Territories council to have it before them. The two resolutions referred to by the minister will, I think bring about a much broader influence of the residents of the Northern Territories. The division, of course, will naturally facilitate this and we are very happy that this will be so. I would hope that this would give us an opportunity to focus more attention on the assistance, encouragement and understanding of the native population throughout the whole of Canada. These people suffer from a lack of understanding. While we are moving ahead, somehow I feel we are not moving ahead as rapidly as we should be in this direction. I would hope that this new division of the territories, and the different governmental set-up, would help to facilitate this understanding in the northern territories.
I am reminded also of the problem of communications. I have long advocated a national highways system. The territories depend entirely upon provincial highways for their communication, and I would hope that the new governments of the territories would press for a national highways system which would give us a far better lead, as it were, into the territories in so far as commercial and tourist traffic are concerned. I might say in passing that we are very pleased to learn a new railway is going up north. I have not any particular personal interest in the matter, but it is of interest to me because one of the contractors from Prince George has a very large contract in connection with the railway. I happen, therefore, to know something about it. Railways are important because they are the only means by which heavy loads can be moved profitably. In this connection, I would think that the value of the resources in the north to Canada ought to give us an opportunity or a reason for looking into the possibility of a subsidy of some kind for freight going in and out of the northern part of the country. I know that the cost of living in some of these areas is very high, and anything that the Canadian people can do to

Northwest Territories Act help get materials in and out of the territories would be a good investment.
I would complete my remarks with these few words. I do believe that the present Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources is interested in these territories, so we can look forward to some very progressive steps in this regard in the near future.

maintopic: RESOLUTION CONCERNING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW TERRITORIES IN THE NORTH
speechtext:
We too, in the New Democratic party, Mr. Chairman, want to indicate our support not only for the resolution before us but for the one which will follow. I would assume that the discussion at this stage will be of such a broad, general nature that the discussion of the following resolution will be extremely brief. Thus, the two resolutions will be passed this afternoon.
We give support to this idea for two reasons. One, of course, is the meeting of the Northwest Territories council and the desire to have copies of the legislation before that body for their meeting. The other reason is based upon our philosophic concept of the rights of people and the need to establish and promote legal autonomy and the legal authority over their political and other activities. These two resolutions lead us in that direction. They move towards the time when people living in the territories will have full control over their own affairs to the same extent as the people living in the ten provinces at the present time.
I listened with interest to the hon. member for Brandon-Souris as he attempted to heap glory upon the shoulders of the Leader of the Opposition for all that the Conservative government did during the past six years. I would say that there has not been that degree of change take place in that period of time to warrant the glory being concentrated upon the members on the Tory benches.
We need to concern ourselves, as has been mentioned, with the economic and social development taking place in those areas now encompassed by the territories. However, we have to keep in mind that any economic and social development that does take place depends exclusively upon the people who are living there. People have to have some emotional attachment to what they are giving themselves to, in order to develop socially and economically to the fullest possible extent. They must have the fullest possible say in their own affairs. There must be legal autonomy. There must be freedom of the individual to determine his own course. All these things go hand in hand. While we believe this step is welcome, in itself, it does relatively little to lead us towards the time when these areas may become elevated to provincial status. There are a number of people of Eskimo origin living within the areas involved and these should be looked at specifically.


We have a large number of native Indian people in Canada classified as such, as distinct from Eskimo people, and our Indian affairs are in a disgraceful and deplorable situation. We are one of the few countries in the world which has a special law designed for a particular group of people, based on their culture and heritage, and if we are not very careful in our approach to the relationship of the Eskimo people in the territories with non-Eskimo society we will find ourselves, in the very near future, in the same deplorable state with respect to the Eskimos that we are in with respect to native Indians.
This is something which should be of prime concern to the minister, his department and the government as a whole. Some extensive research work must be done into the cultural, social and economic problems confronting the Eskimo people in these areas today, and also projected into the future, to make sure we are taking the right steps to preserve the integrity of those people, develop respect for their culture, and within them develop respect for the type of society and economy which we have.
The whole area outside of the provinces in the north is virtually a communist state. When I say that I do not associate it with the situation which exists in the Soviet union, but within that area the federal government has sole, exclusive jurisdiction. Only a few feeble efforts have been made in the past, and are being made today, to break down that federal government, central, authoritarian control. To me this is virtually a system of communism in which everything is directed from the top, and with relatively few decisions being made by those most vitally affected, namely the people who live there.
People in the north tend to look upon Ottawa as a sort of absentee landlord with only some vague, casual interest in road building programs and the like, which take place from time to time. In those parts of Canada which are organized into provinces, by virtue of the British North America Act this tends to place some controls on authoritarianism at the federal level, and this is particularly important in the field of civil and other rights. The closer we can bring control to the people over their own affairs, particularly in matters of rights and freedoms and the direction of their social and economic activities, the better chance we will have to foster a type of democracy of which we can be proud.
Perhaps at present it is not feasible overnight to bring these areas to provincial status. Perhaps they themselves do not feel sufficiently interested or emotionally attached to the concept and idea of becoming provinces, but we must bend every effort possible to

that end, and make sure the time is not too far distant when those areas will become provinces and when the people living in them will have the fullest and highest possible degree of authority over their own affairs. In this way, we can ensure that their social and economic development takes place and moves in a direction in which they want it to, and not in a direction which somebody in Ottawa thinks it should. Perhaps it would be appropriate in this situation to pay tribute to Lincoln's phrase and say that government of the people, by the people and for the people is essential in our democracy, and I hope we can get to that stage at the earliest possible moment so far as the territories are concerned.

maintopic: RESOLUTION CONCERNING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW TERRITORIES IN THE NORTH
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution provides me with an opportunity I have been waiting for since the time I heard that the former deputy minister, Mr. Gordon Robertson, was sent to the privy council, of publicly expressing my gratitude to him for the wonderful job he did while he was in the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, and for his devotion to the development of the north and the welfare of the people who live there.
It also gives me an opportunity to welcome the new deputy minister, Mr. Cote, who I understand will be assuming his duties very shortly. Last, but by no means least, there is another gentleman to whom I would like to pay tribute and who will soon be retiring. I refer to the assistant deputy minister, Mr. Cunningham, who is now sitting in the gallery. I have been associated with all these gentlemen for more than six years. These are excellent men who have acquired a fund of knowledge that is second to none among the experts on the north, and I for one am very sorry to see all this talent departing from the department.
The resolution before us purports to say that legislation will be introduced which will in some way advance the approach to selfgovernment in the territories. There are many people in the north who do not agree with that, just as I do not agree with the hon. member for Skeena when he says that many people in the north look upon the federal government as an absentee landlord. Indeed the reverse is true. They see perhaps too much control from the federal government in Ottawa, and they desire to be as far away from it as they can in the sense that they want more of that control in their own hands.
When my hon. friend from Skeena refers to some vague and casual road building efforts, I suggest to him that he should do a little travelling in the north, which he can do now as a result of the roads built over the
Northwest Territories Act last six years. I further suggest to him, when he says there has been no progress made in the north which would warrant the tribute paid to the Leader of the Opposition by the former minister, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, that he probably forgets the time he visited at my home in Whitehorse and had a cold ade on my patio, which was built by loans made available through N.H.A. and which have resulted in a 200-home development that did not exist in 1957. However, I do not want to get too deeply into that.
I disagree most heartily with the hon. member who interjected when the hon. member for Brandon-Souris was speaking with respect to the vision. He said it was the vision of the Gordon commission; but how many times in the last seven years did we hear it ridiculed, scorned and derided by hon. members over there? How many times have they called the vision a nightmare, and what criticism was heaped upon the things being done in the north? My hon. friend from Skeena speaks about building roads; but I can tell him that in the last seven years almost $25 million were spent on building roads in the Yukon territory alone. These roads brought the discoveries we are now reading about. They include the richest iron ore deposit in the free world, the first discovery of oil and gas in the Yukon, and a tungsten mine. These things have been made possible by communications which were not constructed prior to 1957.
In his introductory remarks the minister made reference to the name Nunassiaq. My hon. friend, the hon. member for the Northwest Territories, is not here but I have spoken with him concerning this proposed legislation, and he tells me the people of the eastern Arctic were given the choice of two names which were suggested by the department. If that is correct, I do not think this is much exercise of free choice, or a selection from 10 names or a selection from 20. Surely the name of the territory should be a reflection of the choice of the representatives of the Northwest Territories people on the council. When we pay lip service to a territorial council in the sense that we have regard to the opinion of these gentlemen who sit on decisions respecting territorial affairs, surely that must be tempered by the realization that the council of the Northwest Territories is not represented at all by any people from the eastern Arctic. No one from that area of the north sits on the territorial council. What is more, the council of nine consists of five members appointed by the minister and only four elected members.
The resolution preceding the bill calls for an increase from four to five in the number of

Northwest Territories Act elected members on this council of nine. This will still leave room for four appointed members. Why not have them all elected; or does the minister feel there are not men of intellect, capability or ability in the north who can discharge the legislative or even the executive functions? Why should there be any appointed members on the council? The Yukon territory now has a council of seven and they are all elected. Surely if in that area we are going to move toward selfgovernment and a full measure of autonomy there are sufficient financial controls so as not to leave the federal government with any fear that their investment is going to be squandered if all members are elected-because monetary control still remains with the department; it still remains with the governor in council.
I am wondering, too, just whose resolution it is that has been tabled by the minister. As Mr. Justice Sissons of the Northwest Territories once said, "The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hand is the hand of Esau". I am just wondering whether the resolution was not drawn up here in Ottawa and presented to the Northwest Territories council and rubber stamped, as good pieces of legislation seem to have the habit of being when they hit the Yukon council. My remarks must be frank here. It would appear that I am the only member from the north, above the 60th parallel anyway, who is going to be speaking on this resolution.

maintopic: RESOLUTION CONCERNING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW TERRITORIES IN THE NORTH
speechtext:
The hon. member for Brandon-Souris says his heart is there, and I agree with him. But I must say that I have grave doubts that the bill which will probably follow this resolution is going to accomplish what the people of the north want.
The minister mentioned that there were three matters which should be considered when discussing legislation of this kind. One was the federal responsibility, the second was the devolution of authority, and the third was the form of government similar to British constitutional practice. I want also to say a word or two about the historical and constitutional background of the Northwest Territories and of territorial government in Canada. In 1905 the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan were created out of the Northwest Territories, as hon. members know, and this transition from a territorial form of government to a provincial one was comparatively easy. It is not so easy to change the system in the north right now, however desirable this might be and however anxious we all are to proceed to that end.
The Northwest Territories Act of 1905, as the minister knows, provided for the liquida-


tion of the affairs of the old government of the Northwest Territories and the appointment of a commissioner who would exercise the executive powers formerly vested in the lieutenant governor or the lieutenant governor in council. The commissioner should administer the government of the new Northwest Territories under instructions from time to time given by the governor in council or the minister of the interior. They remain substantially the same today. Here is where the people of the Northwest Territories are going to have a legitimate complaint with respect to the new territory. It is completely contrary to what I maintain is the law, and certainly the constitutional practice in the growth of governments in this country, to have a commissioner resident elsewhere than in his own territory.
It was suggested by the minister in his opening remarks that the commissioner of the new territory will remain in Ottawa. This has been the complaint for years and years and years in the Yukon territory, and until very recently the commissioner of the Yukon was always an Ottawa appointee. Now he is a Yukoner and is resident there. This was an accomplishment brought about by the former administration which I would very strongly suggest the minister follow with respect to the Mackenzie district when it becomes a separate territory.

speechtext:
I hear the minister say that this will be the case and a local resident will be appointed commissioner. I am glad to hear that. The historical development of the Northwest Territories proceeded from the stage where the governor in council still retained the power from time to time to constitute and appoint a council of four to aid the commissioner in the administration of the territories; but by the passage of the 1905 act the supreme court of the Northwest Territories was disestablished and, as the assistant deputy minister will remember, stipendiary magistrates were constituted for the north. I believe he was one of them. It was not until 50 years later that the territorial court of the Northwest Territories was established. I think this proposal, unless the bill provides otherwise, is going to disestablish that territorial court, as a matter of law. It will be interesting, if the minister will have his legal officers check that proposition, because I believe that is going to be the net result. It appears that by this historical legislative development the government and administration provided for the Yukon and the Northwest Territories by the Yukon Territory Act of 1898 and the Northwest Territories Amendment Act of 1905 follows the precedent of

the Temporary Government Act of Rupert's Land which was passed in 1869. They were presumably enacted to be temporary, and this is the crux of a point that has been made in the past by Mr. Justice Sissons and a point with which I am in wholehearted agreement.
There was some justification at the time of the passage of that legislation for instituting these temporary forms of government. There was a gold rush in the Yukon territory, with thousands upon thousands of people pouring into the area. They were a rough crowd; they were a mixed crowd; they were an international group of people. At that time the Yukon was remote; it had no air lines, no roads, and communication into these areas was slow. There were no highways or railways; everything was in a state of flux. It was necessary to establish immediately a local, stable government for the maintenance of order. At that time, the conditions which made a government seem necessary or excusable existed, but the temporary form of government which was set up then is still in existence. It was set up on the basis that it was to be the government until more suitable arrangements could be made. Now the temporary government of Rupert's Land, which was established as far back as 1867, was maintained for only three years. In the Yukon, the temporary government was maintained for 63 years and in the Northwest Territories for 57 years. This resolution and the resolution to follow it will not remedy the situation at all, because these governments are still not the governments contemplated by the legislation which was passed prior to confederation when Rupert's Land was set up.
There have been various changes both in the Yukon Act and in the Northwest Territories Act since 1898 and 1905 but none of these changes has affected the temporary nature of the institutions which were set up at that time. I cannot agree with the hon. member for Skeena that a communist state exists in the north, because I think such a statement is a disservice to the devotion and industry demonstrated by the departmental officials in their care of the affairs of the north. I will say, however, that it approaches a system of colonial administration. In this regard it seems to me that even the British were much more enlightened with respect to the manner in which they administered their colonies many years ago than we are today. I wish to cite here the words of Sir Saville Garner, a British high commissioner for Canada who wrote an article in the magazine North, which is the official publication of the department of northern affairs. He had just completed a visit, in 1960, to the Northwest
Northwest Territories Act Territories and when he came back he had this to say about the government and the administration there:
Perhaps an Englishman may be pardoned in concluding by making a comparison, which may seem on the surface odd, between Canada's north and the administration in a British colony. Anyone familiar with a colony expects to find a governor who acts not only as the centre of the administration and the stimulus for policy, but also as a focus for all the activities in the territory and as a symbol of its unity. Moreover and obviously the different government services are co-ordinated and work under central direction. While the far north is not a distant island, it does in many ways play the part of Canada's colony; but the contiguity of lands has caused a striking contrast with what is normally to be found in colonial administration. There is at the moment no one at the head of the administration who acts as symbol and is a focus. The commissioner for the Northwest Territories is the deputy minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, who visits the area on relatively rare occasions. The government services, moreover, are not unified.
It seems to me that Sir Saville Garner's words bear a striking resemblance to the conclusion reached by the Glassco commission. I do not agree with all the conclusions of that commission but certainly I am in accord with that which touches the need for a more central government, a government which would be on the spot to deal with northern affairs.
I express this hope to the minister-that the legislation which will be produced as a result of this resolution, and particularly as a result of order No. 7 on today's order paper, will provide for a resident commissioner in the new territory and thus follow along the lines of what, I am sure, was intended by the British North America Act when words were inserted in that measure to provide that the government of Canada would have power to absorb these territories and create them part of Canada for administration and control. This is my view of what the federal responsibility should be in the north. As the deputy minister has often said, the department of norther affairs should be constantly striving to eliminate its reason for existence. Once we have passed sufficient autonomy to the people of the north there will be no further reason for the existence of a department.
It is blithely said that the only difference between the jurisdiction in the Yukon and in the Northwest Territories as compared with that in the provinces lies in the fields of justice, natural resources and the expenditure of money-in other words that although the Yukon council, for example, is fully elected, none of its members can introduce any measure which affects the territorial purse. In reality, much more administrative control is exercised in many more fields than those of justice and natural resources. The hon. member for Brandon-Souris and the hon. member

Northwest Territories Act for Skeena in their remarks mentioned the subject of human resources. When the address was presented to the Queen from the Senate and the House of Commons of Canada, signed by the Speaker of the Senate on December 17, 1867, and by the Speaker of the House of Commons on December 16, 1867-this was the address which contained the terms and conditions upon which the Northwest Territories and the Yukon were placed under the administration of Canada-one of the guarantees contained in that address was that the legal rights of any corporation, company or individual within the territories would be respected and placed under the protection of courts of competent jurisdiction. This, specifically, is why I mentioned to the minister the possibility of disestablishing the territorial court by the passage of any legislation based on this resolution.
The second guarantee which all successive governments since the presentation of that address have left unfulfilled is that which guarantees the Indian tribes compensation for land required for the purpose of settlement. The claims of the Indians, it was said-and here I am reading from the address-would be "considered and settled in conformity with the equitable principles which have uniformly governed the British crown in its dealings with the aborigines". This last condition has not been complied with as far as the Indians and Eskimos of the present Northwest Territories are concerned, nor has it been in the Yukon. There are no treaty Indians in the Yukon territory and it is high time the federal authority did compensate the Indian and Eskimo people of both territories for the use of their land in conformity with the commitments which the Queen and the government of Canada entered into at the time of the address which I mentioned.
May I call it five o'clock?
