speakeroldname: Mr. H. W. Herridge (Kootenay West) moved:
subtopic: POLLUTION
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of the creation of a water pollution control division, composed of representatives of the ten provinces, within the framework of the proposed national resources council, with powers and funds required to institute research programs, collect, collate, and analyse water control data, and to co-ordinate the water pollution control objectives for the provinces, in addition, to further the study of water pollution control objectives for the provinces, in pollution control problems of a national character.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I again introduce this legislation because of the continuing and increasing menace caused by the pollution of our waters to human health, fish and wildlife and to our recreational facilities in Canada, and also because of a growing recognition- and I am glad to say it is growing-of the need for co-operative action between governments effectively to deal with this problem. I know that in dealing with a question like this it can be treated on a strictly nonpartisan basis, because I am certain that there are members in all parties who are seriously concerned with this problem of the pollution of our waters in Canada. There is no need for me to emphasize that the New Democratic party policy stresses the need for the conservation and proper development of our natural resources in order to protect the living standards of this and future generations, and the protection of our waters is a safeguard for one of our most important natural resources.
I am fortunate to live in a country where we enjoy abundant supplies of pure water and clear, mirror-like rivers, lakes and streams. However, many Canadians are not as
Suggested Water Pollution Control Division fortunate as I and have suffered the hazards of water pollution occasioned by the greed of thoughtless corporations and other organizations for generations past. I notice a few hon. members looking at me with a sort of concerned appearance on their faces. I will allay their fears that I may be attempting to introduce prohibition by the back door by quoting from the Philadelphia Monthly magazine of 1798. This is what I read in that magazine:
By its fluidity and mildness pure water promotes a free and equable circulation of the blood and humours through all the vessels of the body... hence water-drinkers are not only the most active and nimble but also the most cheerful and sprightly of all people .. . But to delicate and cold constitutions and to persons unaccustomed to it water without wine is a very unproper drink.
Therefore I hope people will understand our approach to this problem. However, most Canadians today have to depend upon water that is second hand or worse, depending on the stage of its meandering or wandering past industrial plants, municipal intakes and sewers, or through barnyards, ditches or other sources of pollution. This is a problem, I judge from my reading, that has concerned members of parliament and many other people in this country for over three quarters of a century; and yet this menace to life and happiness, and to civilization itself, as history teaches us, continues to grow daily.
While we face this serious situation it would be unfair not to mention or to give credit to those who have worked on this problem almost unsung and unheard throughout the years. There have been a multitude of people who have taken a great interest in this question. Some excellent work in the first instance was done by the international joint commission in dealing with the pollution of the great lakes and other international waters. Some of the work they have done sets a model for other agencies which may wish to follow in the pathway they have blazed. As far as the federal government is concerned several departments are responsible for dealing with some aspects of water pollution. However, the British North America Act as I see it imposes a division of jurisdiction in water management that fails to recognize the interrelationship between various water uses and various water users. This has resulted in a piecemeal approach in dealing with this problem. The tendency at the federal level, and somewhat naturally, has been to concentrate on those aspects of water use specifically delegated to the federal authority in the British North America Act.
The provincial governments have been forced by the growing menace of pollution,
1944	HOUSE OF
Suggested Water Pollution Control Division particularly in recent years, to take some action to meet the problem. For instance, in British Columbia there are several agencies now that deal with various aspects of water pollution. Water pollution has been the subject of very interesting discussions at several British Columbia natural resources conferences. It is now generally recognized by all parties in British Columbia that there is a pressing need for the establishment of a fresh water control agency in British Columbia to deal with the question of water pollution and a need for effective co-operation between the federal and provincial governments in this field.
The Ontario water resources commission was established in 1956 and in co-operation with regional and local authorities there has been some very good work done in this direction. However, they started very late in the day and they have a very large problem to deal with at this time.
In addition, increasing numbers of municipalities have shown concern with the question of water pollution, particularly in the last 10 years. That interest has been stimulated to some extent, I think, by the action taken by the former government in voting $100 million for assistance to municipalities in the building of sewage disposal plants and structures related to the disposal of sewage and so on. I have noticed in my own district that because of the work that has gone on in some municipalities public attention has been more or less focused on the problem, an interest that did not exist before, and I think it is because of the concrete works they have seen being undertaken, as it were, in front of their eyes.
While on the whole we in our district enjoy fresh, pure and clean water, because of growing industrialization in a few areas there is a tendency for pollution to develop. This is causing serious concern, particularly in view of the large scale enjoyment of fresh water. I noticed in a local paper, the Trail Times of May 11, that the association of Kootenay municipalities meeting at Kimberley had a very interesting debate on this question and indicated their concern. Let me say here that the problem is almost infinitesimal in our area compared with what it is in Ontario and other densely settled areas, and I am very glad to see that the municipalities are hoping to take effective action to make certain that pollution does not increase and to remedy any pollution that has developed to date.
The general tenor of the debate at these meetings was the need for co-operation between all levels of government, federal, provincial and municipal. I would say that in addition there is a need for co-operation with many types of community organizations
[Mr. Herrldge.l

because pollution can occur in unorganized districts, in small communities that are unable to deal with the problem effectively unless they have the supporting research and assistance of the senior governments.
In reading various papers I have noted that the problem is receiving attention all across the country at the present time. I am very pleased to see that various periodicals and newspapers across Canada are giving more space to the question of the conservation of natural resources and the question of water pollution. I want to pay particular tribute to the Family Herald, a farm periodical to which I have subscribed for over 50 years. In recent months it has had some excellent articles on the conservation of resources, utilization of land, water pollution and so on. I also wish to pay tribute to the Globe and Mail. I understand it is a Tory paper but it is amazing the number of articles it publishes with which I agree. My reading of the Globe and Mail in the last 18 years has indicated that someone in that organization has a very keen interest in this problem. I also pay tribute to other periodicals.
In particular I wish to mention Mr. Walter Gray of the press gallery who writes for the Globe and Mail and Mr. John Bascom St. John of the same paper. Throughout the years they have written most interesting and intelligent articles on a subject that does not receive enough attention from the press gallery on most occasions. Throughout the years their excellent articles have dealt with various aspects of the conservation of our natural resources. Let me say that their type of journalism is a welcome contrast to the sensationalism that deals with human weaknesses and the sins of the flesh, which have been dealt with so extensively lately, and the foibles of certain sections of our conservative society. I am not going to suggest that we are all saints here. There are some sinners in all parties. I am talking about the failure to understand the value of our natural resources. I must pay tribute to these writers because the people who take the time to write these articles are making a great contribution toward an understanding of the problem and an appreciation of the things that have to be done.
Piecemeal, corrective action to clean up pollution is not enough. The only way to wrest our countryside and our cities from the stinking clutches of pollution is to eliminate the causes and we have not made much progress in that respect to date. To do this, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that several lines of attack are required and I am going to make a few suggestions before I complete my remarks. I am only speaking briefly because

I should like other members who are interested in the subject to have ample opportunity to speak.
I suggest that first of all we need a coordinated federal-provincial approach to water control to unite the present multitude of agencies which work in parallel lines or overlap in federal, provincial and other fields. Second, I believe we have got to have a very extensive research program and this can only be established on the basis of co-operation between governments. Third, we require the collection of water control data, the analysis of water and the collection of other information which can only be done by governments working together. Fourth, when we are dealing with our water resources I think we should establish a sound system of priorities for the use of water. There has been a great failure in this respect in the development of water resources to date. Fifth, I believe that a better relationship, shall 1 say, of water development to ARDA and provincial agencies working in the same field must be established.
In concluding my very brief remarks I should like to quote what a very well known writer has said. I refer to Ralph Tyler Flewelling, who said:
We cannot impose our wills on nature unless we first ascertain what her will is. Working without regard to law brings nothing but failure; working with law enables us to do what seemed at first impossible.
In concluding my brief remarks, Mr. Speaker, I urge support for this resolution on a non-partisan basis to see if we cannot get together to deal effectively with a problem which, to date, has not been met.

speechtext:
This private member's notice of motion, Mr. Speaker, introduced by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) has some merit. I understand that the hon. gentleman has, time and again, sponsored a bill to amend the Criminal Code in order to impose heavy fines on all who are found guilty of polluting interprovincial waters. This was one way of forcing private individuals, incorporated bodies and municipalities to improve this grave situation. Although his bill never passed second reading, I congratulate the hon. member on his past efforts.
The hon. member's new notice of motion is very good, but I must remind the house that the problem of pollution is now scattered over too many departments. By this I mean that we have now the international joint commission, which is made up of an advisory board on control of pollution of boundary waters. This board has four representatives in the United States, two representatives from Canada, four from the state of Michigan,
8, 1963	1945
Suggested Water Pollution Control Division three from the state of New York and three from the province of Ontario. The three representatives of Ontario are connected with the Ontario water resources commission, and the two representing Canada are connected with the Department of National Health and Welfare. The boundary waters concerned are the great lakes and part of the St. Lawrence river.
We have also many other federal departments concerned with this matter. Two other federal departments which are concerned with the pollution problem in Canada are Northern Affairs and the Department of National Revenue. In the past, the Department of Public Works, through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, provided financial aid to municipalities through the National Housing Act. This act assists municipalities in the construction of sewage disposal plants and trunk sewer systems which have a direct relationship to the treatment project. At present, this responsibility comes under the Department of National Revenue.
We have other laws that cover certain aspects of pollution which are related to other departments such as justice, transport, fisheries, public works, etc. The control of the pollution of water is a matter which is dealt with extensively under the law. In addition to the laws already referred to, there are others by virtue of which any person responsible for the pollution of water is liable to be prosecuted. These laws are the Criminal Code, the Fisheries Act, the federal Navigable Waters Protection Act and the Canada Shipping Act. Finally, the Supreme Court of Canada and the common law of the United Kingdom have always declared that riparian owners who complained of pollution were in the right.
Here are a few excerpts from the legislation referred to as found in the Water Purification Board Journal of the province of Quebec:
Criminal Code of Canada
A common nuisance is an unlawful act of omission which ... endangers the lives, safety, health, property or comfort of the public or by which the public are obstructed in the exercise or enjoyment of any right common to all Her Majesty's subjects.
Fisheries Act
No one shall throw overboard ... or cause to be thrown, left or deposited upon the shore, beach or bank of any water... or in any river, harbour or roadstead or in any water where fishing is carried on ... or on the ice over either such water or at a place from which it is likely to be carried into either such water . . . ballast, coal, ashes, stones . . . remains or offal of fish or of marine animals .. . lime, chemical substance or drugs, poisonous matter, mill rubbish or sawdust of any other deleterious substance or thing, whether the same is of a like character to the substances named in this act or not.
Federal Navigable Waters Protection Act
No person shall throw or deposit . . . any stone, gravel, earth, cinders, ashes or other material or

Suggested Water Pollution Control Division rubbish... in any tidal waters... or non-tidal waters ... no owner or tenant of any sawmill... shall throw or cause to be thrown any sawdust, edgings, slabs, bark or rubbish of any description whatsoever into any river, stream or other water, any part of which is navigable or which flows into any navigable water.
Sections of the Canada Shipping Act have been designed to prevent the pollution of water by ships discharging oil from their bilges. I continue to quote:
Supreme Court of Canada
The proprietor of riparian lands has a right... to the flow of water through or by his land in its natural state, and if the stream is polluted by an upper riparian proprietor, the lower proprietor may maintain an action ... for damages.
It is no defence to the person who pollutes to show that the waters were already polluted by other persons. Nor is it a defence that the pollution is the result of business operations carried on in a proper manner and that the business is important to the community.
The rights of riparian owners have always been zealously guarded by the courts. The origin of the common law applicable to this subject goes back and beyond the Roman law.
Common Law
In common law a riparian owner (that is, an owner of land on the banks of a river or stream) is entitled to expect that the water in the river shall flow past his land neither diminished nor increased in amount and without sensible alteration to its natural quality. A riparian owner is therefore entitled at common law (and quite apart from statute law) to take proceedings in the civil courts against any person or body causing injury, interference with the flow of the stream or by polluting its quality.
Thus a riparian owner has only to prove that his right to have the water in its natural state has been infringed to order to succeed in an action: he need not prove actual damage.
Under common law, therefore, almost any water added to a river or stream constitutes pollution.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, it is definitely unlawful to pollute any waters in Canada. However, it would cost the individual a tremendous amount of money in legal fees to enforce this provision. Personally, I feel that the various health departments and other related departments in all the provinces are to blame for the situation that exists today. It is through these departments that permission has been granted to municipalities and firms to dump raw domestic and industrial waste into our lakes and rivers. The various provincial departments have given this permission in past years when most municipalities drew drinking water directly from lakes and rivers by pumping stations without filtration. After epidemics occurred in various areas in Canada in the 1930's, some of the provincial departments issued ordinances to many of the municipalities to build filtration plants for the protection of health. If at that time orders had been issued to build sewage disposal plants, the cost of filtration would have been less and the pollution prob-blem would not exist today. In spite of the


laws that have been in existence for so many years, the provincial departments have closed their eyes and have given permission to pollute waters.
I should like at this moment, Mr. Speaker, to explain a situation which exists in lake St. Louis. The beautiful greenish clear waters of the St. Lawrence river and the mucky, brown polluted waters of the Ottawa river enter lake St. Louis at Ste. Anne de Bellevue and lie Perrot. There exists a distinctive dividing line between the clear, greenish waters on the southern side of the lake and the mucky brown on the northern side which extends from west to east for the entire length of the lake.
All the municipalities which operate filtration plants on the island of Montreal draw this mucky brown polluted Ottawa water except the city of Montreal. The city of Montreal several years ago, spent millions of dollars to extend their intake pipe across the river to reach the clear greenish St. Lawrence waters. The drinking waters of the city of Montreal are of better quality, both by clearness and taste, than that of any other municipality on the island.
All other filtration plants which draw Ottawa waters have to have their filter basins cleaned about seven times more often than that of the filtration plant of the city of Montreal, and also use a very high percentage of chlorine which is self-evident by the taste, compared to that of the drinking water of the city of Montreal. It would cost the municipalities of Pointe Claire, Dorval and Lachine millions of dollars to extend their intakes to the clear waters of the lake, and even if they intended to extend these intakes, the pipes would have to cross the Department of Transport shipping channel. I believe that permission would be difficult to obtain because of damage that may occur from ships.
The reason that we must purify all our lakes and rivers is not solely because of the municipal filtration problems but because of public demand; reasons of health, reasons of aqua life and fishing sports, reasons of bathing beach operations and boating, etc. I believe that the federal government should not make this a confusing problem. To solve this situation, costs should be divided at a ratio of one third federal, one third provincial, and one third municipal for all projects involving water purification, and in addition to this, for all projects where municipalities wish to proceed with building public parks with beach and marine facilities.
The federal government operates many national parks where very few Canadians have the opportunity to go, and I sincerely

believe that it should aid in providing these facilities close to the people who cannot go to Banff or Lake Louise.
Grants for parks with beach facilities should be applicable not only to the building of beaches but also for the expropriation of land for this purpose. The sooner the federal and provincial governments move in this direction the sooner the pollution problem will be taken more seriously.
It will not be solved by another study commission or a division of a department. If the federal government wants a study made on pollution, then all it has to do is issue an order to the research council to study immediately all aspects of pollution in Canada. It is as simple as that; and let us here in this house stop making things too complicated, by forming another board, another department, another commission.
As to the study of water purification in the province of Quebec, this study has been neglected for many years. Dr. Kirkland, who was a member of the Quebec legislative assembly for Jacques Cartier riding for 25 years sounded the alarm amongst the public about the plague of water pollution. Each year at each session he brought the subject up, but not until the year 1960, when the Liberals took office under the fine leadership of Premier Lesage, was action taken.
Premier Lesage gave Dr. C. A. Kirkland the task of settling this problem. In spite of his failing health, Dr. Kirkland proceeded with bringing forward bill 88, which created the water purification board. He postponed from day to day his trip to a Boston hospital by continuing his discussions with Premier Lesage and putting finishing touches to bill 88, so as to have it ready for the coming session. He has fallen victim of his duty, and the population of Jacques Cartier, for whom I am the federal M.P., are grateful to him for his endeavours.
The legislative assembly of Quebec gave unanimous approval on June 1, 1961 to bill 88. Hon. C. A. Kirkland passed away on August 8, 1961. He was succeeded to the legislative assembly by his charming daughter, the Hon. Claire Kirkland-Casgrain, minister of state, who was the first woman ever elected to the legislative assembly in the province of Quebec.
I am proud to add that I was one of her staunch supporters. Last year, Claire Kirkland-Casgrain organized all the 17 municipalities in my riding to form a vigilante committee. Despite the intentions of municipalities to build treatment plants, we went a step further and asked municipalities to pass by-laws which will prevent shore pollution, by prohibiting individuals from dumping any foreign matter into the lake. When I see each

Mr. Speaker, I just have a few words to say on this important matter, and one of the considerations which draws me into the discussion is to congratulate the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) upon his persistence and perseverance in this vital renewable resources area. Over the years he has introduced this resolution, dealing with conservation generally, and now specifically with the problem of water pollution. He and the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) have been pioneers in this conservation area. I suppose one could call them good Conservative conservationists.
However it does provide us with an opportunity once again to give attention to what is perhaps one of the most critical problems in the whole area of renewable resources. As a result of the difficulties in considering our rich heritage of resources we, as I have said many times before in this house, brought together the resources for tomorrow conference in 1961, which had as its basic focus the necessity for the wise management and multiple use of renewable resources. It cannot be repeated too often across the country that that conference charted a whole new course in this very difficult area.
The previous speaker mentioned the essential difficulty resulting from the problem of divided jurisdiction. Our resources, including water resources, belong to the provinces, and down through the years in a federal state we have had the drawback of log rolling, Ottawa throwing the problem to an individual
1948	HOUSE OF
Suggested Water Pollution Control Division province and the province in turn throwing it back to Ottawa. Nothing was done until we held the resource conference in 1961. I am sure the hon. member who is sponsoring this resolution is aware of the buck-passing technique which delayed action on his perennial motion, for example. Some encouraging action and progress has been made in recent years and, legislation already exists on the statute books dealing with this difficulty of divided jurisdiction. The most important act in this respect is the Canada Water Conservation Act which provides for federal participation in major water control measures, participation of up to 33-J per cent. The usual formula results in participation by the provinces to the extent of another 33J per cent, leaving the rest to be handled by the municipal authorities. This act has been on the statute books for a number of years-at least ten, I believe-but was only used in recent years. In late years several major water control programs based on the wise management and multiple use principle have gone forward in Canada. I refer to the metro-Toronto water control program, which is a multimillion dollar scheme. Any province can participate on this scale if the province itself is willing to seize the initiative, because the federal legislation is available. It is up to the province to effect intragovernmental coordination among the departments at the provincial level, having co-terminus jurisdiction in the resource field.
Then, of course, the sewage disposal legislation has gone a long way to dealing with the immediate problem of pollution of our water by reason of the disposal of raw sewage.
I think the most promising development, however, in this field is the resource ministers council. This is just under way and, if it continues to make the progress that it has made during recent months, it will be a most useful organization in resolving this perpetual difficulty of divided jurisdiction in a federal state.
I agree with the previous speaker that we do not need any more boards; we do not need any more government departments. We do not need any more conferences. I think it will be agreed that the resources for tomorrow conference, with the three volumes which resulted from the deliberations, will provide enough grist for the resource mill at all levels of government for many years to come. To refer to the resource ministers council, which came into being a year ago last September at a meeting in the city of Toronto, this council represents a new type of federal-provincial co-operation in that it stresses the spirit of co-equality. While the federal minister is represented he is, to use
(Mr. Dinsdale.]

a phrase that was frequently referred to ur-ing the preliminary stages of formation of the council, co-equal with his provincial counterparts serving on the council. In other words, it gets around the difficulty that always arises from federal-provincial programs, where the provinces feel they are being pushed around. How many times during recent years, during the very active period of co-operative federalism, have we heard protests from provincial governments that Ottawa is intruding itself too directly into the affairs of a province because of these participating programs. I feel that the genius of the resource council is simply that it places the participating ministers in the position of co-equality.
We have been assured by the minister of northern affairs that the next step forward is about to take place. This is the setting up of a secretariat which will work with the council of ministers to do the necessary research and provide the background of information that is needed, because of inadequate research hitherto, in all the renewable resource areas. Pollution, for example, could be referred to this secretariat; they would be the research centre and the sounding board that could exhaustively examine the problem, and on the basis of their conclusions the governments concerned could take action.
I think the present executive set-up of the council is most auspicious in this respect. It is going to establish its headquarters in Montreal; it will be the first perfectly bilingual governmental agency. It is neither a federal body nor is it a provincial body; it has equal responsibility to both these senior levels of government. The principle of a rotating chairmanship has been adopted. This is also an excellent idea because, while the federal minister started out as the chairman of the resources for tomorrow conference and while he continued as the chairman of the coordinating committee of ministers that emanated from that conference, the decision was made to get away from this tendency on the part of the provinces to feel they are being pushed around by Ottawa, by having a rotating chairmanship. The first chairman after the federal minister, who had chaired the pre-conference steering committee and the post-conference provisional committee, was the resource minister from Ontario, the Hon. Mr. Spooner, and the current chairman is the Hon. Rene Levesque who has co-operated in all respects during the organizational stage of this important resource ministers council. He will be followed, I would presume, by the minister from Prince Edward Island; and

eventually on the basis of this annual rotational system every provincial minister will have the opportunity to chair the council. I sincerely trust, Mr. Speaker, that a general secretary of the secretariat will soon be appointed. It was encouraging to hear from the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) that some excellent candidates have applied and their applications are now being processed. I am sure that before very long we will have a permanent secretariat operating with the resource ministers council and this council, in the days that lie ahead, will make a major contribution to resolving the problems that are dealt with in this excellent resolution.

Mr. Speaker, I should commence by expressing my commendation of the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), who once more has demonstrated his unflagging zeal and enthusiasm to protect one of our priceless national assets, the streams and lakes of this country. There are, as I see it, two aspects of the resolution which is before us. In the first place the resolution deals with the necessity for research and survey. I believe-and I say this with great respect for the hon. member for Kootenay West-that we should co-ordinate with this resolution an executive body that can enforce the findings of such research and survey. I realize this may take us into the jungle of constitutional dispute.
As I understand the law, sir, there is power vested in the dominion government under the criminal law, and with regard to health and safety, to make prohibitory legislation. I realize the right of prohibition is of course not the same as the power to regulate. I realize, also, that within the province there can be no dispute about the provincial power to regulate in regard to provincial streams. But we are dealing in this resolution with the question of interprovincial streams and lakes and there is then the question as to whether the power of the provinces remains unimpaired in this regard.
There are many interests concerned in this resolution. There are the riparian owners; there are the rights of fishermen, casual and commercial; the rights of municipal authorities and the federal parliament. Living as we do in this industrial age I believe it is inevitable that we accept that trade effluent will be discharged in our streams and rivers. It follows, logically, that we must take full necessary steps to treat these effluents adequately. I would recommend to this house that we adopt the example of the United Kingdom where, as I understand it, a water control division has been set up to ensure that no one can discharge trade effluent into
Suggested Water Pollution Control Division a stream or a body of water without permission from the water control board. Firms must submit a written application stating the amount of effluent they propose to discharge, the maximum daily amount and the anticipated amount over a year. The board then considers the flow of water in the stream, the nature and the quantity of the effluent and other related factors before deciding whether or not to grant a permit. A permit cannot be unreasonably withheld and there is a right of appeal to the courts if a board makes an unreasonable decision.
I suggest we must permit elasticity in the standard of purity or pollution which may exist not only in various streams but within the stream itself, in various parts of its course. The same standard of purity cannot be maintained in an industrial part of our country as could be expected in sparsely populated regions. So the problem is twofold. We must try to maintain the purity of those streams which have not yet been polluted and we must attempt to restore those waters where pollution has already taken place. I suggest we must have an executive body with adequate powers for these purposes and I believe such a body could be set up by agreement with the provinces. This may require the provincial governments delegating certain of their powers with regard to interprovincial streams and that, of course, raises the question of the British North America Act. I am convinced the whole matter of pollution control must proceed in a spirit of co-operation, good will and patience. It is going to take a good deal of money to clear up the rivers, streams and lakes of this country.
I trust the house will forgive me if I mention a constituency point. I am speaking about the necessity of constant surveys. It often happens that streams and waters are polluted, and those using them do not realize it. For many years that part of lake Erie which abuts the riding of Brant-Haldimand was a source of supply of valuable white-fish and pickerel in commercial quantities. Then, almost overnight, the fish disappeared and today we can only catch perch in these waters-a fish which does not offer a profitable return to our fishermen. Had adequate research been carried out and regular surveys been conducted, this pollution would have been detected before it had accomplished this destruction.
I said a while ago that there had to be good will and co-operation in this matter of attacking pollution. The government has before it at the present time a program designed to encourage industry to go to areas where there is high unemployment. If we initially impose upon industry a high standard of
1950	HOUSE OF
Suggested Water Pollution Control Division sewage treatment, should they relocate in accordance with this program, a high capital outlay would be required. This might well discourage such firms from helping the government to achieve its purpose by moving industry into depressed areas. I would respectfully suggest that the government should consider granting tax incentives to industries required to make substantial capital outlay on treating effluents in order to maintain the purity of our water.
I do not propose to trespass further on the time and patience of the house. I will only say, once more, that this will take co-operation, good will, a great deal of money, above all, patience.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF FINANCE ON BUDGETARY PROPOSALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should first like to thank hon. members for allowing me to make this statement at this time.
Since the budget was brought down on June 13 the government has received representations and suggestions for changes from members of all parties in this house and from many people outside. The old saying that only he who wears the shoe knows where it pinches has always been as true of taxes as of most things. The complexity of modern business and, therefore, the complexity of modern taxation, has made it increasingly difficult for governments to foresee all the administrative problems and all the consequences of tax changes. Detailed information, from those affected, can be secured only after the proposals have been made public. No government and no minister of finance should be reluctant to reconsider and revise proposals if public discussion shows it to be desirable.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF FINANCE ON BUDGETARY PROPOSALS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
I might say that there are, of course, many recent precedents for so doing.
On this occasion I acknowledge with gratitude the representations and suggestions that have been made. All have been carefully considered. Some are good ideas which I am glad to act on. Therefore, on behalf of the government I am proposing to table tonight revised resolutions on the Income Tax Act and the Excise Tax Act to supersede those tabled on the night of the budget. In part, what the revisions do is to clarify the budget proposals and improve them in detail. For example, we had recommended that sales taxes would not have to be paid by the purchaser under a fixed-price contract; it should have been made clear that a binding tender, submitted before the budget, would also be regarded, if accepted, as equivalent to a contract.
There is another administrative change of a similar kind. We had proposed to set a time limit of 12 months-that is, until June 14, 1964-before which deliveries of building materials, machinery, etc., under existing fixed-price contracts must be made in order to qualify for refund of sales tax. Although that time limit is adequate in the majority of cases it is not unreasonable, I think, that it be extended to December 31,
1964.
Information received from various industries since the budget was delivered makes it clear that the exemption from sales tax on materials consumed or expended in a manufacturing process should be continued. The tax would bear inequitably on many manufacturing enterprises and on the printing and graphic arts industries. The resolution has been modified accordingly.
It has also been revised to operate more fairly as between those who construct buildings on the site and those who manufacture pre-fabricated buildings or certain pre-fabricated components of buildings.
A different type of clarification in the income tax resolution concerns the question of appeal, which was raised early in discussion in this house. It is the government's intention that the powers sought in order to prevent "dividend stripping" and the use of associated companies to reduce tax should be made subject, in the bill, to appeal to the Exchequer Court. This has been incorporated in the resolution.

The proposed definition has been changed in a number of ways. The requirement that 25 per cent of the company's directors shall be Canadians will not come into effect until 1965 and will be broadened to include resident officers of the corporation. And, to meet the cases of corporations with widely-spread ownership who would have great difficulty in determining the beneficial ownership of shareholdings, they will be able to qualify if their shares are listed on a Canadian stock exchange and not more than 75 per cent of the voting stock is owned by a non-resident shareholder or others associated with him.
This requirement provides for a substantial minority interest, available to Canadian investors, as a counterweight to a controlling group with interests outside Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF FINANCE ON BUDGETARY PROPOSALS
speechtext:
It is proposed that materials used in their construction will continue to be exempt from sales tax, in effect, by the refunding of the tax on a basis similar to that followed in the case of hospitals.
The issues involved in a decision such as this are extremely difficult ones for a minister of finance. Any tax produces hard cases. It is often tempting to think that we should deal with them by allowing an exception. But if we should follow that impulse we would in no time end up with a tax system which is too complicated to be administered well, and which does not produce the revenue needed.
For this reason, if exceptions and exemptions are allowed to go too far, they do more harm than good.
Nevertheless, after careful reconsideration I think it right to make such an exception in the case of schools and universities. Their need for new buildings is so great, they are

Statement on Budget Proposals of such importance to the future of Canadians, and the sources of finance available for their construction are already so strained that they are a very special case indeed, and one that, on reflection, I believe should be recognized.
The second change that the government proposes is one that has, in the short run, a considerable effect on the revenue that will be raised. I should therefore remind the house of the objectives of the budget which was presented on June 13th.
It is, first of all, a budget designed to encourage production and employment. To achieve those purposes we must accept a deficit while our economy expands. But if we are to have full employment and economic growth, not only in the short run but on a sustained basis, we must reduce the excess of our current payments to other countries over receipts from those countries. Such excess expenditure abroad does not produce any employment in Canada. That is one reason why we must export more and compete more effectively against imports.
Moreover-and this is the second main objective-we must take positive action to safeguard the Canadian economy against an ever-increasing and excessive degree of ownership and control outside this country. This must be done while we continue to treat fairly the foreign investors who are making-and, I hope and believe, will continue to make-an essential contribution to the developement of our country.
These objectives cannot be gained without maintaining confidence in our economy and our finances. For that reason, we cannot contemplate an indefinite series of budget deficits. It must be clearly established that our fiscal policy and measures are so designed that, when other forces are strong enough to cause the economy to operate close to its full capacity, our budget will be balanced.
These are the interrelated objectives of the budget. They are not simple or easy. But I think they are objectives to which most responsible people will subscribe.
They mean that, in present circumstances of production and employment it is reasonable to budget for a substantial deficit. But they also mean that the government must take definite action to reduce the deficit as production and employment increase. That reduction will not come about quickly enough solely through the natural expansion of government revenues. The growth of Canada implies growth in our expenditures also. Many of the new programs which Canadians clearly want for their well-being, and which are needed for economic expansion and the creation of more jobs, will require increased expenditures next year. We must be in a posi-

tion to meet those needs. We must therefore provide for new sources of revenue, especially for revenue that will come to us next year.
I have explained to the house why removal of the exemption from sales tax on building materials and machinery is, in my opinion, the least objectionable source of additional revenue.
At the same time, the evidence that has been presented makes it clear that the sudden imposition of the tax at the rate of 11 per cent would have a very sharp immediate impact on some industries. Of course, there are always objections to raising any tax, even from many of those who feel most strongly that the budget should be balanced. The government cannot accept such pleas to eliminate the tax. But full consideration of the arguments suggests that the timing of the extra taxation can be adjusted in a way that will synchronize with the needs of the economy over a longer period.
It is proposed, therefore, that the tax will come into effect in stages. The rate charged from June 14th will be 4 per cent. This will continue until 31 March next year. The rate will then be raised to 8 per cent and will continue at that level until 31 December,
1964.	After that the final 3 per cent will be added.
Refunds will be made to those who, during the period from June 14 until tonight, have actually remitted sales tax at the full rate on goods they have sold or imported that were previously exempt.
The graduation of the tax will have two effects. First, it will give people time to adjust their affairs, to absorb the impact of the tax in the most convenient way. Second, the graduation of tax rates will provide an important incentive to people to proceed with construction and other investment projects now.
The total result of the revision in the resolutions will be to reduce revenues, compared with the estimate I made on June 13, by about $115 million in the remainder of the current fiscal year. For the full fiscal year 1964-65 we estimate that the additional revenues previously forecast will now be $125 million less.
As Minister of Finance I regret the loss of revenue during the next 18 months but I believe that on balance the changes now proposed will be helpful. They do not alter the objectives of the budget. They will improve its immediate economic effect and stimulate expansion and employment. The resolutions I am now tabling contain the details of the changes I have mentioned and some minor or consequential changes I have not mentioned. I would propose they be

printed in today's Votes and Proceedings for the convenience of hon. members, that is the amendments which are proposed in the budget resolutions.

Statement on Budget Proposals
The situation with which we are confronted tonight, Mr. Speaker, is one which has never happened before in the House of Commons. The house has had to dispense with the ordinary business with which it would have been dealing at this time, and we have had to agree unanimously to postpone the business so the Minister of Finance could explan the inexplicable, define the undefinable and bring forward, as I said, the fourth chapter in the budget. Sometimes he has done this during the course of a budget debate. Sometimes he has done it during discussion on the budget resolutions. Usually, these changes have dealt with minor, technical matters. For the first time since Canada became a nation in 1867 we have had a minister of finance review his whole

budget and explain that this was misunderstood, that was unworkable, this was administratively difficult, and that should be postponed.
We have had a discussion of the budget. First we had the budget speech itself and then we had an amendment moved by the official opposition. We had a debate on that and we had a division. On the division one party, the Social Credit party, frankly supported the government and voted against the opposition, against us, on the amendment. The other party further to our left did not vote, and I was somewhat reminded of a certain president of a certain country who many years ago said he was too proud to fight. I think on that occasion the party to our left were too proud to vote. In any event they did not vote. But the fact remains that the official opposition voted against the budget and parliament, after that division and over the protests of the opposition, accepted the budget. Now, what do we have?
We have the Minister of Finance coming into the House of Commons tonight. As I said, I do not blame him too much. He was put in an absolutely impossible position, in the time limit imposed, in the way he was circumscribed and in the instructions which undoubtedly he received from the government of which he was an honoured member. We are not particularly criticizing him at this time, although obviously he has to take a great deal of the responsibility.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we are having this debate tonight, not on any formal motion, I would suggest, but by the unanimous consent of the House of Commons to revert to motions so that the Minister of Finance might attempt to explain what had been unexplainable and not understood heretofore by the people of Canada. We all know that the word "motions" appearing in our rule book is a catch-all phrase which enables a government, ministers of the government, those sitting on the treasury benches, to make explanatory statements, usually about matters which have not yet been before parliament itself. Indeed I think this is the first time in the history of parliament when we have had "motions" used to enable the Minister of Finance to deal with substantive motions which had already been dealt with by parliament. This, sir, I say is an affront to parliament, and it is by a party which talks about its loyalty to parliament.
I suggest to you, sir, without indulging in any partisanship whatsoever on this _ very non-partisan occasion, that when the history of this parliament is written on the occasion of the centennial which is only a few years away-

As I have said, Mr. Speaker, I think some consideration should be given to whether or not this is an affront to parliament itself, parliament having debated the budget during the regular period, having considered amendment and having finally, rightly or wrongly, made its decision. Then tonight we have statements brought in of such an order and of such a nature that I certainly do not propose to deal with them in any detail at this time.
If anything, this shows confusion and disorder on the part of a government which was going to give us decision and firmness in parliamentary procedure. After all, without getting too technical, the Minister of Finance admits in his statement-and I give him full credit for it-that the balance of ways and means is substantially affected by the statement which he has now brought in. It is reduced by the order of $150 million, according to what my right hon. friend, the Leader of the Opposition, whispers to me.
I would suggest to you, sir, and I draw this particularly to the attention of the house leader, the Secretary of State, that there have been previous occasions when other ministers of finance, not of the government opposite but in the relatively immediate past, attempted to give statements with respect to the financial transactions of the government. Mr. Speaker, you of course being non-partisan and impartial, and not remembering any debate that goes on from one day to the other, could not be expected to recall these things; but even the Prime Minister, and the Secretary of State-in one of his non-partisan moments, if there are such moments-might remember when I attempted to deal with financial affairs affecting the economy and I was told never to do it on motions, but to go into ways and means. I was told that this might affect the balance of ways and means, and the only way it could be done was through a motion that you, Mr. Speaker, leave the chair and that the house resolve itself into committee of ways and means.
My immediate predecessor, the former hon. member for Eglinton, was confronted with this argument; but tonight, by the co-operation of the members of the opposition and entirely contrary to all rules respecting fiscal controls of this nation, we have had a debate on motions which should only have been countenanced on a motion that you, Mr. 28902-5-124J
Statement on Budget Proposals Speaker, leave the chair and that the house resolve itself into committee of ways and means.
After hearing the statement of the Minister of Finance tonight, it is obvious that this whole budget should have been withdrawn. Indeed to all intents and purposes it has been withdrawn. It has been staggered. The days of its coming into effect have been postponed, and there has been one step after another to alleviate the burdens which were imposed by the budget. Tonight we have a situation where the only way in which the government should have cleared up the situation would have been to bring in a new budget, to withdraw the old one, and have a motion put that you, sir, should leave the chair and that we should have a committee of ways and means.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF FINANCE ON BUDGETARY PROPOSALS
speechtext:
I wonder whether the doubts
and uncertainties of the past few weeks have been resolved, or has the minister by his statement tonight made a bad matter worse and made still more clarification necessary? He has tried to clarify-and I will give him full credit for attempting to do so-some of the doubts; he has tried to answer some of the many questions which have been raised across this nation. But in so doing I am wondering whether he has not left more unanswered than he has answered, and in trying to answer the questions he has tried to answer I wonder whether he has not created new ones. The only way these questions can be resolved is by dealing with the resolutions themselves.
I am not going to deal with the subject matter of the resolutions to which the minister referred. Obviously some of them are of a technical nature. The minister was good enough to send the resolutions to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and myself and, I presume, one or two other hon. members. He sent the details to us before he spoke about them, and we thank him for so doing. But the amendments are so technical and so numerous, and are of such an effect that certainly one could not be expected to deal with them tonight.
We have the one about building materials. We are glad to know that universities and schools are going to be exempt from the impact of the tax. It certainly did not need a soothsayer or prophet to know this would be done. Someone once said that Joseph Howe was neither a prophet nor the son of a prophet. One did not have to be a prophet or the son of a prophet to anticipate that change tonight. That was obviously one that was going to be made. Many of the others which the Minister of Finance brought forward were obvious, but the impact on the over-all picture is such that we need a great deal of time and mature consideration to decide just what will be the over-all impact. The matter of machinery and apparatus is another item which is of course parallel to that of building materials.
The minister also went quite a way in another direction, certainly in so far as the graphic arts and newspapers are concerned. That was a fairly obvious change also. There was no question as to what was going to happen in that direction and one would be very naive if he did not think there would

be any amendments in regard to this item. We have heard of certain amendments with respect to materials consumed and expended directly in the process of manufacture. That clause was a sleeper; it certainly went a lot further than the minister or the government realized when they brought it in. They just looked at the capital letters and they had no one to explain what this clause meant. They took the capital letters covering machinery and apparatus to be used in the manufacture and production and did not look at the fine print, which is much more important, because a printing machine, printing press mill, or whatever it may be, may or may not be taxable. They taxed it. You can accept it if you feel it is justified, or you can oppose it. It is a positive thing. Then there was material consumed or expended purely in the process of production. There you had the sleeper of all sleepers. You had the protests of the graphic arts industry and the newspaper publishers which were vocal, pointed, direct and justified. There are hundreds of industries in this country which are suffering and will continue to suffer from that provision; make no mistake about that. I would think a further amendment has to be made there if we are going to deal with this problem.
Then we have, of course, another area in the budget which does not attract popular attention because it deals with finance and the stock market, the buying and selling of securities and investments. The great majority of our citizens are perhaps not too much interested in this question. But this nation- and I am sure the Minister of Finance has said this from time to time-depends now, and will for many years in the future, upon a constant inflow of a reasonable amount of foreign capital. Frankly I think the Minister of Finance has an exaggerated opinion on this matter, but he has stressed again and again the necessity of Canadians controlling their own instruments of production.
We would all agree with that. We all welcome that as an ultimate goal. But when a nation is in a situation as precarious as the one in which this nation is today, needing capital in substantial quantities from day to day and from year to year, let the hon. gentleman remember that we can cut out building this building, or that building, and the tax on building material may set back 10,000 or 100,000 people and put them out of jobs; but if you once stop capital flowing into this nation, the troubles which happened in April last year in connection with our exchange position will be like an April shower compared with what would happen as a result of this budget. Not only would the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) be buried under the avalanche which would follow but
Statement on Budget Proposals the economy of this nation would be buried as well. That is why I say the necessary thing for this house to do, as soon as a reasonable interval has elapsed in which to study these resolutions-and I am not, now, spelling out how long that interval should be-would be to go into committee and get down to a detailed study of these proposals so that parliament and the nation may finally know where we stand economically in the coming year.

Mr. Speaker, first of all, I should like to tell the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) that we are very pleased to see him back with us and that we greatly appreciate his presence in this house where he always conducts himself with dignity and kindness. I can assure him that we appreciate that. It is also worthy of note that members of the cabinet have missed him, that they have often been caught unawares and, as much as possible, have avoided answering questions asked in the house. It is to be hoped that, now that their leader is back, the members of the Liberal cabinet will have regained their poise and their high spirits and will give us the answers to which we are entitled.
I should like to point out, in passing, that on the occasion of the Prime Minister's return, the Minister of Finance has treated him not to a shot of Gordon dry gin but to one of Gordon dry tax.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with a remark made by the financial spokesman of the Conservative party before talking to the new resolution the Minister of Finance has just presented. He did not miss the opportunity to say that we had supported the government when the budget was adopted. In that respect, I wish to set him straight. We did not support the government, we gave it a chance to submit its resolutions, its estimates to the committee of the whole house, so that we could make suggestions to improve them, if only a little, as is the case tonight. Besides, the Conservative opposition seems to forget that all last year we supported it until February when we fell under that heavy load.
We are ready to give a chance to whatever party to present legislation and submit to the house matters likely to interest it.
We are going to make suggestions and we hope that they will be welcome.
Some of the changes which were recommended this evening are of an administrative nature and will involve minor changes only. In our opinion, little has been changed

Statement on Budget Proposals in the budget. However, there are two things which command our attention and we felt it would be a good thing to point them out. The Minister of Finance stated that the 11 per cent tax will not apply to materials used in the construction of schools, colleges, universities and buildings of a similar nature. The government deserves to be commended in that respect, because we feel it is the proper attitude to take, but it has forgotten some items. There was some talk about exempting from the 11 per cent tax the building materials used in the construction of churches, monasteries, etc. The Minister of Finance has overlooked that point.
I also note that political personalities in Canada had called for an exemption from that 11 per cent tax on materials entering in construction projects carried out by municipalities, provincial crown corporations and governments.
Only a few days ago, Mr. Rene Levesque said that this tax would paralyse us and that it would cost the province of Quebec from $25 to $60 million within the next five years. What can the Minister of Finance and the present government reply to this man from the province of Quebec who is trying to develop industry?
After the decisions announced tonight, what will the present government reply to the mayor of Montreal, Mr. Jean Drapeau, who stated recently that the 11 per cent tax on building materials would cost $30 million to the city of Montreal during the next five years? What will be the reply of the Minister of Finance to the C.L.C. or to the national confederation of labour unions? The levying of the tax is postponed, it is applied gradually; I only hope that the delay the Minister of Finance has provided for himself will enable him to ascertain that this tax is effectively disastrous to our national economy and that he will abolish it.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to be content to criticize; I would like to help the Minister of Finance in finding a solution. It is not enough to criticize; what we need are solutions. It is obvious that the minister finds himself faced with a dilemna, which he sums up in the following passage of his speech:
Of course, there are always objections to raising any tax, even from many of those who feel most strongly that the budget should be balanced.
In short, we see that the Minister of Finance has but two alternatives; taxes or budget deficits. But deficits entail debts, and debts
[Mr. Gregoire.l
lead to high interest rates. And what about the $918 million that we shall have to pay this year on our present debt?
Mr. Speaker, I am not able to say whether it was done on purpose or not, but the Minister of Finance seems to have limited himself to two fields: taxes and deficits which means taxes and debts.
I wonder why the Minister of Finance who is known by the people of this country as an intelligent man is not looking for a third alternative or is not trying to find a solution to the problem we are facing at the present time? Why is the Minister of Finance always faced with two alternatives: either to increase taxes, which involves a slowing down of our economy and an increase in prices, or budgetary deficits and indebtedness?
Mr. Speaker, I suggest to the Minister of Finance that he try to widen his vision because, in this day and age, we are facing new problems as we are living in a new era and we must find new solutions.
In my opinion we are through with taxation and deficits, which offer no solution.
If we stay in that rut where there are only those two alternatives, it is natural that we will get hurt, and the Liberal party seems content to remain in that narrow path. The Minister of Finance is not getting out of the rut. He must try to find another solution, because inevitably, as he said himself a moment ago, our economy will again be unbalanced because the country is expanding. Our population is increasing, our assets are growing and the Minister of Finance will, under such circumstances, of necessity have to submit another deficit budget.
But why should we have an expansion involving debts to private concerns, debts which burden future generations? Why would not that deficit instead be assumed by the people's financial organization, a body which belongs to the people and which would not saddle future generations with the payment of interests such as ours has to pay?
Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of Finance had his deficit financed by the Bank of Canada, which belongs to the Canadian people, and not by the chartered banks, which belong to a few individuals who control the progress and development of this country, he might well afford to increase his deficits. Indeed, on the day when the Minister of Finance accepts to consider that third solution, he will not appear before us saying:

"Unfortunately, we will have to increase taxation, otherwise the deficit will be too high."
If, at this time, the minister defers this tax, because it hurts, he will only defer the blow, or, to say it briefly, postpone the day of reckoning. It is a respite, it is true, but a respite which may mean an unstable currency. There was often a question of inflation in the past. Well, that 11 per cent sales tax, even if progressively increased, even if deferred, indeed, means inflation. I think that the minister was well able to see that the imposition of that tax resulted in higher prices. As a matter of fact, I received a telegram from the officers of the home builders' association of the Montreal district, which said that the tax would entail an increase of $850-and not $400

in the building costs of a home.
Mr. Speaker, it should be kept in mind that when prices go up, money loses its value, and this causes nothing less than inflation. I remember very well that during the last election campaign, some people suggested that Social Credit policy would lead to inflation. I ask the Canadian people whether it is we who are bringing about inflation at the present time. It is rather the Minister of Finance and his government, through the imposition of the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials.
I wonder whether the minister has thought of what will happen in a few months when the tax will increase. It is possible that for some time a few Canadians might be able to hoard building materials, but only those who will enjoy enough credit to pile up such materials in their warehouses and their factories.
On the other hand, small contractors and house builders who do not have the necessary margin of credit to pile up materials, will have to pay a heavy price when payments fall due, because they did not have the means to hoard building materials, for lack of credit facilities while rich and powerful contractors will pile up materials and be in a position to indulge in competition which I declare forthwith illegal, because they will have taken advantage of the privilege now granted by the government. And it is really a privilege which is granted to a few financial tycoons by suggesting to them: "You who can pile up materials, do it immediately, because the sales tax on building materials is only 4 per cent whereas in six months or a year, it will reach 8 or 11 per cent."

On the other hand, those who have not the necessary credit or are not sturdy enough, financially speaking, will not be able to accumulate materials and, in a year and a half, will be definitely under unfavourable conditions, so much so that the small building contractor might disappear.
Mr. Speaker, I admit that there is some good in the measure, as it aims at delaying the bringing into force of the sales tax but, on the other hand, one must clearly understand what it will entail shortly-that is when the tax will be raised to 11 per cent for all the small building contractors. They will have to close shop, for they will then be unable to face the competition that is being set for them at present.
Mr. Speaker, there is a solution to the problem and it must be found. It must be found outside the paths followed by economists of the past. It must be found with something reflecting the realities and the possibilities of our time. In brief, we must face present realities, that is the tremendous capacity of the Canadian people to develop the country and to produce. That is what is physically feasible.
We now ask the Minister of Finance to turn aside from the beaten track in order to reform our economy, not in a production sense because private enterprise sees to that, not in the field of consumption, because the Canadian people see to that, but in a third field, that is the field of exchange, the monetary field of the economy.
In fact, I urge the Minister of Finance not to ignore the solution, not to fear deficits, but on this condition only that his deficits be financed by a Canadian organization, an organization which belongs to the people, that is the Bank of Canada. If those deficits are financed interest free, they will not impose a burden on future generations. On the contrary this generation will be in a position to develop the country without having to support the burden of taxes and to bequeath our successors a still greater country.
Mr. Speaker, that is why, before concluding my remarks, I should like to impress on the Minister of Finance that we are living in a modern age because of new methods of production, because of the tremendous progress that has been achieved.
So, he must enlarge his vistas, extend his fields of investigation, search beyond the orthodox economic principles of yesteryears to find a new solution where he will not

Statement on Budget Proposals always be squeezed between the two walls of taxes and deficits which will allow him to find a third outlet to develop the economy of the country, that is an economic system, a monetary system really belonging to Canadians and which will enable them to develop their country for the benefit of Canadians, by Canadians and for Canadians.

speechtext:
-who must have been anticipating with some trepidation having again to navigate very rough waters without the skipper at the helm.
We heard a lot about a baby budget before the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) came into the house this evening. I suppose you might call it that. If so, it is a very attenuated baby, a very minor baby. The final difficult birth resulted in triplets, but not by any means identical triplets. As I say, there is not a great deal to this. It was, as most people expected, a retreat in some form as far as was considered possible, with the great necessity of saving face on the 11 per cent sales tax. Most of us, I think, will certainly support the Minister of Finance when he exempts schools and universities from the imposition of this tax. Certainly there is some satisfaction in seeing that the tax is going to be imposed in stages, although it occurs to me
[Mr. Gregoire.l
that the Minister of Finance may find himself again subjected to a flood of correspondence from customers who have been charged a high price for their purchase, who have paid a tax on it and are applying for a refund. I wonder just how he is going to deal with those people who have bought paint to paint the front porch and who had to pay the sales tax which the entrepreneur is now going to get back in his hands again.
But, Mr. Speaker, there are great omissions in the exemptions that one would have hoped for in the statement of the Minister of Finance. There is, for instance, only a very limited exemption with respect to housing which is not only one of the major social problems of the country but also one of the major means by which economic activity is stimulated. Also, sir, there is no suggestion that the great construction projects on which expansion depends are going to receive similar treatment. In fact, they are rather rigorously left out of the statement submitted to us.
What I was particularly interested in was the last few sentences in the minister's presentation tonight in which he said:
As Minister of Finance, I regret the loss of revenue during the next 18 months but I believe that on balance the changes now proposed will be helpful. They do not alter the objectives of the budget. They will improve its immediate economic effect and stimulate expansion and employment.
That is a truly charming expression. The budget is to be improved, and it has been improved undoubtedly, by taking the exact reverse position from that which the minister took less than a month ago. It seems to me that if these retreats do as the minister suggests tonight, stimulate expansion and employment, then the budget as a whole, as I said earlier in the house, is not calculated to stimulate employment or expansion. In fact, Mr. Speaker, the most depressing thing about this final triplet of the triplet budget, if it is final as one of my colleagues says, is that it reveals that the Minister of Finance is still wedded to the philosophy in which he drew up his budget originally. It is defined fairly well in the statement he made on July 2 of this year in reference to something that the leader of this group had said. At that time the minister said, as found on page 1751 of Hansard:
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam would like to see our budgetary deficits increased. He argues that if consumer expenditures are increased this will in turn increase the general level of economic activity throughout the country. I say to him that the trouble with this theory as applied to Canada-and I say this with respect because I am not unaware of the theory; I understand it, I think-is that about one quarter of such increased expenditure, or so it is estimated, would find its

way into additional imports of one kind or another and this would aggravate our payments problem and only add to our difficulties in the long run.
That, of course, is quite true when we have a government that is determined to do four things. It is determined to expand production and to increase employment. It is also determined to balance the budget, to maintain a fixed rate of exchange and to cope with our balance of payments problem. I would suggest this to the Minister of Finance. While it may be quite true that under conditions of a fixed rate of exchange any increased government expenditure may very well have the effect that he suggests in his comment to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), the same is also true of any other expansion of payments, any other expansion of income, any increase in employment, any stimulation of the economy. I am driven to the conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Finance tonight has merely confirmed the suspicion that some of us have had all along, that this budget was not designed to expand the economy. This budget was designed to control exchange crises while at the same time maintaining a fixed rate of exchange, which I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, is incompatible with any expansionary move in our economy.
If the Minister of Finance is still so concerned about coming somewhere close to a balanced budget and if he is looking for other sources of revenue, I suggest to him there is another place he may look for some of it at least. These figures are contained in statistics produced by the dominion bureau of statistics on the 4th of July this year. They give figures for business gross savings from 1958 to 1962 but I will just give the increase from 1961 to 1962. The increase in depreciation allowances and miscellaneous adjustments from 1961 to 1962 was $216 million. The increase in undistributed profits in the same period was $201 million.
I might point out that in his budget the Minister of Finance is contemplating adding to these depreciation and depletion allowances for certain extremely well heeled industries in this country. Therefore I suggest that if the Minister of Finance is unable to accept the theories that are accepted by most modern economists of an expanding economy and the use of deficit financing to achieve that end, if he is going to base all his activities on the possibility of a balanced budget some time, these are some of the sources that he should consider, rather than bringing to a halt, as he apparently is still going to do, a vast number of major projects on which the welfare of the Canadian people is going to depend in the next year or two.

It seems to me there are three courses open to the house and to the government. One would be to get unanimous consent either from the house at some proper time, or preferably from the committee of ways and means, which is already seized of the resolutions.
