speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the committee rose at five o'clock I was attempting to draw an analogy between what the situation should be in the Northwest Territories and what I hope will be in the legislation which will be produced following this resolution. Perhaps the minister might well have referred to the situation in Manitoba, and perhaps a comparison might be drawn from the time when Manitoba became a province.
The territorial government, just prior thereto, was presided over by a resident commissioner. The seat of the government was in the territory, and there was a lieutenant governor appointed by the governor in council. I believe that person was a Mr. Morris, who held office during pleasure, and whose duty it was to administer the government under the jurisdiction from time to time given to him by the governor in council or the secretary of state for Canada. This is similar to the situation today. There was a legislative assembly composed at first of 26 members altogether, who were the elected representatives of the electoral districts with powers similar to those given to other legislative bodies, much in the same way as the powers are given to the Yukon under the Yukon Act and the Northwest Territories under the Northwest Territories Act.
The legislative assembly could not adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address or bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue or of any tax or impost to any purpose that had not been first recommended to the assembly by message of the lieutenant governor in the session in which such vote, resolution, address or bill was passed. This is similar to the provision today in the Yukon Act and the Northwest Territories Act, and therein lies the control by the federal government over these expenditures in the north.
There was an executive council, and here I think that there is an important distinction, to aid and advise the government of the territories; and the persons who were to be members of the council were, from time to time, chosen and summoned by the lieutenant governor; and the members thereof might, from time to time, be removed by the lieutenant governor. By statute, 36 Victoria, chapter 6, the membership of the council was increased to a maximum of 21 instead of 15, the minimum remaining at seven. Members of the executive council were made the heads of and presided over the departments of government in the territories. At that time they consisted of, first, the office of the executive 28902-5-125*
Northwest Territories Act council; the department of the attorney general; the department of the territorial secretary; the department of the treasury; the department of public works; the department of agriculture; the department of public instruction and the offices of the legislative assembly.
The public service was divided into two divisions. First, there was the inside division consisting of the employees comprising the several departmental staffs at the seat of the government in the territories. Second, there was the outside division comprising all other employees of the government of the territories. The system of civil service in both territories is under the complete and absolute discretion of one man who is under the direction of the minister, and here I refer to the commissioner himself. He has complete authority as to who shall be hired and fired, but there are no formal ground rules laid down for competitive examinations such as those that exist in the civil service of Canada. The staff of each department was divided and ranked similar to the divisions and ranks that pertain in the federal civil service.
The conclusions I would like to draw here, Mr. Chairman, in the hope that they will be taken into consideration by the minister and his officials, are that pursuant to the joint address presented in 1867, at a time when the Northwest Territories were admitted into the Dominion of Canada, certain guarantees were given. Further, the terms and conditions under which the Northwest Territories were admitted into Canada were not complied with, and are still not complied with so far as the Northwest Territories and their existence today are concerned, and incidentally neither in so far as the Yukon territory is concerned. This conclusion carries with it very far reaching constitutional effects which are being dealt with from day to day in our courts.
Second, there have not been formed in the Northwest Territories, according to the terms of the joint address, those "political institutions bearing analogy, as far as circumstances will admit, to those which exist in the several provinces of this dominion." This is very clear if one analyses the types of government that have been set up in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon territory, as compared with those which prevailed immediately prior to the creation of the various provinces of this dominion.
Third, and it is quite important, the claims of the Indian tribes for compensation for lands required for purposes of settlement have not-again in the words of the joint address-"been considered and settled in conformity with the equitable principles which have uniformly governed the British crown
1964	HOUSE OF
Northwest Territories Act in its dealings with the aborigines." Surely this legislation should provide for some relief here, and I am glad to see the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration present in the chamber because this should be of particular concern to him.
There was a treaty at one time with the Indians of the Mackenzie district, but it was never really implemented and has become a dead letter for all practical purposes. Further there has never been a treaty implemented with the Indian people of the Yukon. There has been no treaty with the Eskimos, and no relinquishment of the lands reserved to them as their hunting grounds by the treaty of Paris of 1763. There is no Eskimo act and the Indian Act does not apply to Eskimos.
The time for provincial autonomy is still probably a good many years distant so far as certain portions of the Northwest Territories are concerned. However it is rapidly approaching so far as the Yukon is concerned, and even so far as the Mackenzie district is concerned. At this stage I want to interject that I do not hold with those who believe the two territories should be joined because they have different geographical problems, and their historical traditions, forms of government and their economies are quite different. It appears we are not ready for it yet in the Northwest Territories, but if we are going to take steps towards achieving autonomy, surely these steps should be in accordance with the constitutional practices which have prevailed in Canada since and immediately prior to confederation.
My own recommendations, which I hope the minister and his officials will take into consideration are first that the House of Commons should set up a special committee to examine all aspects of both these resolutions, Nos. 6 and 7 on today's order paper; and since they have not been invited to participate in any of the discussions, the people of the eastern Arctic should be consulted because they live there. They are the people who pay the taxes in that area, and they are the people who are pioneering in that area. Their views and opinions should certainly be sought as to whether or not this is the kind of legislation they desire.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to speak for very long on this resolution tonight because I am sure we all want to see it carried. But coming from Edmonton and having had a personal interest in the north for some time, I hope that I may make some slight contribution on the resolution stage, because I want to consider the manner in which we should look at the bill when presented.
The minister said in his opening statement that the people of the Northwest Territories were noted for their responsibility and courage. While I will agree with those complimentary terms, I think that perhaps the initiative shown by those people is something the house should consider as more important. I say this for the reason that we are all aware to some extent of the natural disabilities faced by people who settle in that north country. These disabilities, as we all know, are the extremes of climate, the very few people around, the lack of conveniences, the great distances from any markets, etc. All these disabilities require a type of person with a great deal of initiative, and all of them make it necessary that the government, in regulating the lives of the people up there, must allow as much flexibility as possible so that changing conditions which exist from place to place, the difference in people themselves, and so on, may be dealt with by those on the spot who have the experience, the drive and the ambition that took them there and who can figure out, because they are so close to the problems, a way to get around these things and have more room to manoeuvre.
This is where I think we run into a good deal of trouble in the north occasionally. I

Northwest Territories Act do not want to be too critical of the civil servants there, but it does seem to me that there is a natural attitude on the part of a civil servant who is, for instance, interested in the welfare of the air force in a particular area, to get just a little bit narrow in his outlook and concentrate so much of his energy on air force matters that it is easy for the well being of the civilian population to be not only overlooked but perhaps trampled on to some extent.
In the Northwest Territories this is what can happen most easily, because government employees constitute really the majority of the people there. There are people employed by the northern affairs department, the Department of Transport, air force people concerned with defence, northern transportation people, and Eldorado people. By the time you consider all the government people in the north you find they constitute the majority of the population, and therefore any attempt to regulate from Ottawa is perhaps going to have the effect, whether intended or not, of putting the welfare of the government department first and the welfare of the ordinary civilian second; or should I put it this way, of being government for the sake of government rather than for the sake of people.
I suggest to the minister that it is his responsibility in that territory to remember this fact about the Northwest Territories, that while paternalism by civil servants may show up in any place, the Northwest Territories is the most fertile ground for this to happen, in that because of the preponderance of civil servants, and because of the vast distances, we may see more examples of this happening.
I have had occasion to speak previously in this house on regulations made by the air transport board, for instance, where you have long distances, a small amount of business really, high costs and few people involved. A regulation made by the air transport board to strengthen the air industry, while it may be very suitable as a general policy for all of Canada, may in fact have a very detrimental effect on that particular part of the territory. I suggest, therefore, that what is needed is an acceleration of the reliance of people in the north on their own self-government.
The minister spoke of the responsibility of those people. I have talked about initiative. Surely these two factors are very important and useful in government. I must say that the development of the north shows we have been very slow in taking advantage of the tremendous amount these people could do to govern themselves. There seems to have been a feeling that we should take it easy because there are few people there and development is slow. I suggest that perhaps it is because we have taken it easy that development has
(Mr. Nugent.]
been slow. Perhaps we should exercise less caution in this regard and lean more heavily on these people than we have in the past.

speechtext: I do not know that I can accomplish what the hon. gentleman has in mind other than to indicate that there was an all-party agreement that this discussion would conclude today. I might also suggest that the matter which has been raised by the hon. member could be better discussed in a committee of the house, if such a committee were set up, because it involves a matter of detail. It would be possible to have officials before such a committee and the question could be clarified to the satisfaction of all concerned.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, GOVERNMENT, AND ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
If this committee were set up before the bill is presented, I would accept

Nunassiaq Territory
the proposal. I think we could make some good suggestions on this point. I am rising because this is a most important matter. To whom will these islands belong? Will they belong to the federal government or to the provincial government? That is my point in speaking on this resolution. I am convinced they should belong to Quebec, and if they are to be included in this new territory I cannot accept it. If the committee is ready to sit and the Secretary of State can assure us that it will sit before the bill is presented, then we will agree.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, GOVERNMENT, AND ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
speechtext: I do not think it would be possible to sit before the bill is presented, but I am sure we could make some arrangement to have the matter considered before the bill is proceeded with. What we want to get is the first reading of the bill so that it can be seen by the Northwest Territories council; but we would not proceed to second reading for a good long time. I would be quite prepared to give an undertaking that in some fashion or other this matter would be remitted to a committee so that the matters the hon. member wishes to raise could be raised, if that is satisfactory.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, GOVERNMENT, AND ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Might I point out to the hon. member for Lapointe that we are particularly anxious to have the resolution stage passed so that we can get a copy of the bill for study during the summer, to present it to the council that is now meeting at Inuvik. It is particularly desirous that a copy should be released to them for study. I might point out to the hon. member that while he protests the possibility of certain measures being contained in the bill, when he sees the bill he might be entirely satisfied. Certainly the production of the bill, which we would like to produce tonight, is a prelude to any study by the committee. I would confirm the undertaking given by the house leader that we will have a committee set up suitable to the hon. member where these matters can be discussed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, GOVERNMENT, AND ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
speechtext: We agreed to let the resolution pass and have the bill presented to the house, but the point I was making was this: If we could bring forward suggestions before the bill was presented perhaps the government could introduce an amended bill to the house. I can assure the minister of national resources that we will see that just treatment is given. But I am convinced that these islands belong to the province of Quebec and should be included within the territory of the province of Quebec.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, GOVERNMENT, AND ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Shall the resolution carry?
[Mr. Gregoire.l

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, GOVERNMENT, AND ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to inquire what consideration the minister intends to give to the suggestion made by a number of members for the establishment of a committee of the house to go into the whole problem of the Northwest Territories, as it affects these resolutions and others.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, GOVERNMENT, AND ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
speechtext: It is proposed in the commitment given by the house leader that if it is unsatisfactory that a committee of the whole deal with the matter, and there is a demand by the committee of the whole for a special committee, I am certain we will be happy to have a special committee set up.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, GOVERNMENT, AND ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
speechtext: The committee of the whole would not allow representatives to be heard from various agencies, who I am sure would want to be heard by a special committee established for the purpose. I think there is a considerable difference. The house will go into committee anyway, but I think the solution is much broader than that. I want to know whether this matter can be given consideration.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, GOVERNMENT, AND ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
speechtext: I will give the hon. gentleman the assurance I have already given the hon. member for Lapointe, that once these two bills are seen, if there is any demand from any quarter of the house that some of the matters in the bills or other matters related to them could usefully be reviewed by a committee, I will undertake to ask my colleagues to have this done, and I feel sure they would agree with me. In fact I am quite prepared to commit the government to putting a motion on the order paper for a reference to a suitable standing committee of the house to consider these matters before we proceed with the legislation itself. This could be done, unless hon. gentlemen would be equally well satisfied when they have seen the bill to having it read a second time and then having it sent to the committee for revision. I will undertake to discuss it with hon. gentlemen and meet their reasonable wishes in the matter.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, GOVERNMENT, AND ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
speechtext: I should like to make now a formal demand for a special committee on this bill. Is that agreed?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, GOVERNMENT, AND ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
I think the hon. gentleman would perhaps find that he is restricting himself in the way he puts that, but I do not think there is any real misunderstanding between us.
The Depuiy Chairman: Shall the resolution carry?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT, GOVERNMENT, AND ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Carried.
Resolution reported and concurred in.

Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Would the house leader announce the business for tomorrow?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The business for tomorrow is the business for today which we never reached; that is to say, second reading of the Atlantic development board bill. I hope we can get both second reading and committee stage through tomorrow, so that we can send the bill to the other place and make progress
Business of the House with this matter. When we have completed that we will take the second reading of the economic council bill, and should there be any time before the end of the day we will take the resolution preceding the measure respecting the Department of Agriculture.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The business for today, which the house leader mentioned, would have been reached had not the government had to revert to motions to make further corrections to some of its other mistakes.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That was understood when the business was announced and agreed to on Friday.
It being ten minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
